terms.gloss: Author of the book being introduced, a Russian journalist and writer
terms.why_hard: Name transliteration must be fixed once; also he's the author, not a subject, so framing matters

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social network founded by Pavel Durov in 2006
terms.why_hard: Must decide between transliteration 'VKontakte', abbreviation 'VK', or keeping the branded form; zh readers need an analogue cue

proposed.zh: VKontakte（俄罗斯最大的社交网站）

terms.gloss: Recurring metonym for VKontakte via its blue logo
terms.why_hard: Recurs as a stand-in for the platform; literal 'blue-azure' vs simple 'blue logo' affects tone of the synecdoche

terms.gloss: Dismissive label: 'a nature preserve of schoolkids' — 'shkolota' being derogatory slang for obnoxious teenagers online
terms.why_hard: 'Школота' is mid-2000s Russian internet slang with contempt built in; 'школьники' would lose the sneer

terms.gloss: Common accusation that VKontakte merely copied Facebook
terms.why_hard: Needs Facebook rendered recognizably per language; the scare-label nature must be preserved, not presented as fact

proposed.ja: 「フェイスブックのクローン」

terms.gloss: Ironically distanced reference to 'real life' as opposed to online life
terms.why_hard: The irony ('so-called') must carry over; flat 'real life' loses the author's smirk at the distinction

terms.gloss: Bureaucratic-academic phrase: 'the history of the question', i.e., the backstory of the whole matter
terms.why_hard: Literal rendering reads oddly in English; it's a set phrase signaling mock-official register

proposed.en: the backstory of the whole thing

terms.gloss: Generational regularities — the idea that a generation's habits inevitably take over
terms.why_hard: Must sound like pop-sociology, not hard science; the mock-solemn register is the point

proposed.en: the simple laws of generational succession

terms.gloss: Held forth with visionary zeal / theorized grand plans (ironic corporate-intellectual jargon)
terms.why_hard: Standard Russian is 'мечтал' or 'строил планы'; this is an anglicism parodying high-minded tech visionary posturing.

terms.gloss: An online platform / site / venue for interaction
terms.why_hard: Could be mistranslated as a physical venue or playground rather than an online hub/platform.

terms.gloss: University departments / faculties (specifically of Saint Petersburg State University)
terms.why_hard: In US English 'faculty' means teaching staff, whereas in Russian/European universities it denotes a major academic department/school.

terms.term: создадим иллюзию, что все уже здесь
terms.gloss: Fake-it-till-you-make-it tactic of simulating an active initial user base to create critical mass
terms.why_hard: Losing the cynical growth-hacking calculation behind the phrasing.

proposed.en: create the illusion that everyone is already here
proposed.zh: 制造所有人都在这里的假象
proposed.ja: 誰もがもう参加しているという錯覚を作り出す

terms.gloss: Influential students / opinion leaders / informal student authorities
terms.why_hard: Can sound purely corporate ('key personnel') if not balanced with the student context.

terms.gloss: Forum moderators with administrative powers over discussions
terms.why_hard: Easy to translate literally, but its role in early 2000s forums carried prestigious social status.

terms.gloss: Tossing an orange back and forth as an idle dorm pastime during dialogue
terms.why_hard: Syntactically inserted as an action-beat without a verb; requires natural narrative framing.

proposed.ja: オレンジを放り投げる

terms.gloss: Their existing local platforms (separate departmental forums, IRC, guestbooks)
terms.why_hard: Needs to convey the fragmented ecosystem of pre-existing student sites across SPbGU.

proposed.ja: 自分たちの既存フォーラム

terms.gloss: Internet message board / discussion forum (the dominant social web architecture in 2006)
terms.why_hard: Modern readers might equate it with contemporary social media feeds rather than phpBB-style bulletin boards.

terms.gloss: Meet other students / mingle with folks
terms.why_hard: 'Народ' here is colloquial youth slang for 'other people/students', not 'the Russian nation'.

terms.gloss: Alternative centers of power / student factions / informal authority structures
terms.why_hard: A grandiose geopolitical term deliberately repurposed for student politics/networking.

terms.gloss: The tenant / room renter (referring to Ilya Perekopsky, who rented the flat)
terms.why_hard: A reader might not realise this refers to Perekopsky in his shared student flat rather than Durov.

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, Durov's university friend, future vice president of VKontakte
terms.why_hard: Must match standardized book-wide transliteration/spelling across chapters.

terms.gloss: The orange fruit, stylized poetically/abstractly as an orange sphere
terms.why_hard: Could be misinterpreted as an actual toy ball rather than the orange mentioned earlier.

terms.gloss: Flicked the light switch (to go to sleep)
terms.why_hard: Standard idiom, but sets the final mundane contrast to grand ambition in the scene.

proposed.ja: 部屋の明かりを消した

terms.gloss: Domain name of the unofficial SPbGU student portal founded by Pavel Durov in 2006
terms.why_hard: Needs to be preserved verbatim as the historical domain name.

terms.gloss: Forum software engine (specifically phpBB in Durov's case)
terms.why_hard: Slang for software engine/CMS, distinct from search engine or car engine.

terms.gloss: Nikolai Durov, Pavel's older brother and technical genius/architect
terms.why_hard: Nikolai is an essential figure in VK/Telegram history; the unstated identity should stay subtle but accurate.

terms.gloss: Tweaked / patched / made minor adjustments to code or settings (from auto-body straightening)
terms.why_hard: Colloquial mechanical metaphor applied to software hacking/tweaking.

terms.gloss: An ordinary, unremarkable forum like any other
terms.why_hard: Russian idiomatic duplication indicating typicality/standardness.

proposed.en: a forum just like any other
proposed.ja: ごくありふれた掲示板

terms.gloss: Deus ex machina, an external arbiter intervening decisively to settle disputes
terms.why_hard: Direct calque of 'deus ex machina', used metaphorically for an omnipotent administrator.

proposed.ja: デウス・エクス・マキナ（機械仕掛けの神）

terms.gloss: Checks and balances (manipulating rival factions against each other)
terms.why_hard: Constitutional law metaphor used here to describe Machiavellian community management.

proposed.ja: 牽制と均衡（チェック・アンド・バランス）

terms.gloss: Supreme Moderator (ironic quasi-theocratic title for Durov's forum persona)
terms.why_hard: Must preserve the pompous, mock-imperial capitalised or solemn tone Durov cultivated.

terms.gloss: Carefully construct one's public persona / cultivated mystique
terms.why_hard: 'Образ' here means cultivated persona/public image, not artistic image or mental picture.

proposed.ja: パブリックイメージを綿密に構築する

terms.gloss: picaresque or adventure novel genre framing Durov's biographical arc
terms.why_hard: translating mechanically as 'adventurous novel' rather than the literary genre 'adventure novel' or 'picaresque'

terms.gloss: fairy-tale-like metamorphoses / transformations of character/status
terms.why_hard: sounds like literal magical shapeshifting if not tuned to biographical metaphor

proposed.ja: まるでおとぎ話のような変貌

terms.gloss: in pure defiance of and across/against the grain of the system
terms.why_hard: colloquial Russian idiom pair combining 'out of spite' and 'athwart/contrary to'

proposed.en: out of sheer spite and against the grain of the system
proposed.zh: 故意对着干、逆体制而行
proposed.ja: システムへのあてつけと徹底的な反逆

terms.gloss: break down constraints/boundaries imposed from outside
terms.why_hard: cliché in Russian that needs natural non-wooden idiomatic equivalents across targets

terms.gloss: defy expectations regarding one's behavioral logic
terms.why_hard: can be mistranslated as negative 'disappoint' instead of strategically subverting expectations

terms.gloss: armored mega-yacht, an oligarch archetype trope in post-Soviet imagination
terms.why_hard: missing the satirical post-Soviet oligarch trope evoked alongside pop stars

proposed.ja: 防弾仕様のメガヨット

terms.gloss: Lady Gaga, quintessential Western hyper-pop celebrity used here as absurd status prop
terms.why_hard: grammatical inflection in Russian ('какой-нибудь Леди Гаги') expresses generic, flippant dismissal

proposed.ja: レディー・ガガの如きセレブ

terms.gloss: controlling stake in Gazprom, symbol of ultimate Russian state-capitalist oligarchic power
terms.why_hard: omitting corporate/political weight: Gazprom is the quintessential state monopoly

proposed.zh: 俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司的控股权
proposed.ja: ガスプロムの経営権（過半数株）

terms.gloss: an attic/garret on Nevsky Prospekt, evoking St. Petersburg bohemian aesthetic and Durov's base
terms.why_hard: failing to recognize both the specific St. Petersburg architectural trope and VK's actual headquarters location

proposed.ja: ネフスキー大通りの屋根裏部屋

terms.gloss: drawing dogs; reference to Durov's famous mascot dog drawing (which became VK dog/Spotty)
terms.why_hard: treating it as random whim rather than specific allusion to VK's iconic white dog mascot

terms.gloss: 'to be continued', serial novel/film formula applied to living biography
terms.why_hard: flat literal rendering loses cinematic/serialized narrative punchline

proposed.zh: 欲知后事如何，且看下回分解

terms.gloss: Yury Saprykin, influential Russian cultural critic and intellectual journalist of the 2000s–2010s
terms.why_hard: transliteration conventions and recognizing him as the foreword/blurb author

proposed.ja: ユーリー・サプルィキン

terms.gloss: Rambler-Afisha, major Russian media holding company uniting tech portal and cultural guide magazine
terms.why_hard: translating as separate words instead of recognizing the specific combined 2010–2013 corporate brand

proposed.ja: ランブラー・アフィーシャ

terms.gloss: Prologue; marks start of main narrative voice and St. Petersburg street scene
terms.why_hard: structural section heading requiring standard book typography alignment

terms.gloss: Kazan Cathedral and Kazan Square on Nevsky Prospekt, opposite the Singer House
terms.why_hard: the text leaves the cathedral unnamed, assuming Petersburg topography knowledge

proposed.en: the cathedral and the square in front of it
proposed.ja: カザン大聖堂とその前庭広場

terms.gloss: Nevsky Prospekt, the central avenue of St. Petersburg
terms.why_hard: Russian uses 'проспект' elliptically because Nevsky is self-evident in this setting

terms.gloss: flâneured, strolled leisurely in city flâneur tradition
terms.why_hard: translating as simple 'walked' loses the French-derived Petersburg literary register of flânerie

proposed.ja: 気ままにそぞろ歩いていた

terms.gloss: university study cohort/class group, typical social unit in Russian higher education
terms.why_hard: misinterpreting as a casual bunch of friends rather than an academic study group/cohort

terms.gloss: Singer Building (Dom Knigi) on the corner of Nevsky Prospekt and Griboyedov Canal, VK HQ
terms.why_hard: unnamed in this opening sentence; careless readers miss that this is the legendary Singer House / VK headquarters

proposed.en: the mansion on the canal corner
proposed.ja: 運河の角に建つ瀟洒な洋館

terms.gloss: the suburbs/outskirts of Hades, Greek mythological realm of the dead
terms.why_hard: translating as generic 'hell' loses the classical myth underworld resonance set up by 'строй теней'

terms.gloss: a line/host of shades (ghosts of the dead in Hades)
terms.why_hard: mistaking for literal silhouettes/shadows rather than mythical ghosts of the underworld

terms.gloss: Soviet-era petty factory thieves pilfering parts/materials to resell

terms.gloss: Prepared question sets or study answers for examinations in philology subjects.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering such as philological tickets is unintelligible outside the Russian university system.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the future founder of VKontakte, recalling his behavior at school.

proposed.ja: 恐怖そのものを恐れる

proposed.zh: 基督复临安息日会信徒在课桌前排练圣歌

proposed.ja: この波乱万丈めいた環境

terms.gloss: Steve Jobs

proposed.ja: スティーブ・ジョブズ

terms.gloss: Bill Gates

terms.gloss: Linus Torvalds

terms.why_hard: Opaque outside Russian literary tradition; needs a gloss rather than transliteration.

proposed.en: resoner (the didactic speechifier of Russian literature)
proposed.zh: “议论者”(俄国文学中好发议论说教的角色)
proposed.ja: レゾネール(ロシア文学の持論を振りまく講釈師)

terms.gloss: Colloquial 'disses everyone, trashes everyone indiscriminately' — provocation as performance.
terms.why_hard: 'гнать' here is street slang for talking trash, not literal movement.

proposed.ja: 誰彼かまらずこき下ろす

terms.gloss: Ivan Goncharov, author of 'Oblomov' (1859), the classic Russian novel glorifying idleness.
terms.why_hard: Surname alone doesn't tell a foreign reader he's the novelist; must be linked to Oblomov.

terms.gloss: Oblomov, the famous lethargic aristocrat-hero of Goncharov's novel, archetype of Russian laziness.
terms.why_hard: Adjective 'милый' (endearing Oblomov) is the point; needs consistency as a book-wide archetype.

proposed.ja: 愛すべきオブローモフ

terms.gloss: Stolz, the energetic German-blooded entrepreneur in 'Oblomov', whom Durov calls mechanical.
terms.why_hard: Durov inverts the usual reading (Stolz as ideal) — translator must preserve that contrarian twist.

terms.gloss: 'our wondrous country' — ironic stock phrase for Russia.
terms.why_hard: Irony would be lost rendered as sincere praise.

proposed.ja: この素晴らしき我らが国

terms.gloss: Recurring character, evidently Durov's classmate/interlocutor at school.
terms.why_hard: Book-wide consistency of a minor recurring figure's name transliteration.

terms.gloss: Fyodor Dostoevsky, whom the teenage Durov calls 'a terrible writer'.
terms.why_hard: The scandal lies in dismissing a national monument; name must match canonical target-language spelling.

terms.gloss: Chekhov's last play (1903) about an estate's cherry orchard sold for lumber.
terms.why_hard: The class fight over Lopakhin vs Ranevskaya assumes the plot; target languages have established title translations.

terms.gloss: Lopakhin, the merchant in 'The Cherry Orchard' who buys the estate and cuts the orchard.
terms.why_hard: Durov's contrarian defense (man of action) against the children's intelligentsia disdain must stay legible.

terms.term: купечество… влезшее сапогами в кружевную душу Раневской
terms.gloss: Schoolkids' image: the merchant class stomping its boots into Ranevskaya's delicate lace soul — allusion to Mayakovsky's 'past one o'clock…'.
terms.why_hard: Echoes Mayakovsky's 'still coarser-booted than Pushkin's verse'; if flattened to plain prose, the whole debate loses flavor.

proposed.en: merchants barging in booted into Ranevskaya's lace-work soul
proposed.zh: 商人阶级穿着长统靴踏进郎涅芙斯卡娅蕾丝般的灵魂
proposed.ja: 商人階級が長靴でラネーフスカヤのレースのような魂に踏み込んだ

terms.gloss: Ranevskaya, the impoverished genteel landowner of 'The Cherry Orchard'.
terms.why_hard: Casting her as victim requires the reader to know her role; transliteration consistency needed.

terms.gloss: 'man of action/deeds' — a stock Russian value category opposed to dreamers and idlers.
terms.why_hard: A set phrase in Russian cultural argument; should not be paraphrased ad hoc.

terms.gloss: Pre-reform landed gentry estate owners (as a class), blamed by Durov for ruining the orchard.
terms.why_hard: Has no exact target-language equivalent; must be class-accurate, not just 'landowners'.

terms.gloss: The class nearly came to blows over the play.
terms.why_hard: 'передраться' is brawling school slang; register must stay colloquial in a serious biography.

proposed.ja: 危うく殴り合いになりかけた

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the founder of VKontakte and the subject of the biography.
terms.why_hard: His surname and full name must be romanized consistently throughout the book.

terms.gloss: An ironic epithet for a car as a proud product of mass motorization.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering may miss both the mock-heroic tone and the fact that Durov is retaliating against a car.

proposed.en: that worthy offspring of the motor age
proposed.zh: 这个汽车化时代的骄子
proposed.ja: 自動車化時代の申し子

terms.gloss: The disused airfield where Durov used to sit and read, later taken over by development.
terms.why_hard: It may refer to a specific St Petersburg site whose identity and capitalization should be checked against other segments.

terms.gloss: Consumer society personified as the force replacing open space with shopping developments.
terms.why_hard: The phrase is polemical here, not the Russian institutional term for a consumer cooperative.

terms.gloss: Gigantic shopping malls likened to Babylonian monuments of excess and hubris.
terms.why_hard: Rendering it merely as large malls loses the biblical image and the author's contempt for consumerism.

proposed.ja: バビロンさながらの巨大モール

terms.gloss: A privately or semi-privately operated minibus running a fixed urban route and collecting fares onboard.
terms.why_hard: It is neither an ordinary taxi nor exactly a municipal bus; the chosen equivalent must preserve its post-Soviet social setting.

proposed.ja: 乗合ミニバスのマルシュルートカ

terms.gloss: Durov's asserted student entitlement to ride public transport without paying.
terms.why_hard: The legal or practical basis of the supposed entitlement must be checked, since the sentence may reflect his own expansive interpretation rather than an actual universal right.

proposed.en: a student's right to free travel

terms.gloss: The minibus driver characterized as a large, intimidating bruiser.
terms.why_hard: A neutral phrase such as big driver would lose the implication of physical menace.

proposed.ja: 大柄で威圧的な運転手

terms.gloss: The driver's conventional demand to know who has not passed their fare forward through the minibus.
terms.why_hard: Without the marshrutka custom of passengers handing money along the cabin, a literal who didn't pass it on is opaque.

proposed.en: Who hasn't passed up their fare?
proposed.ja: まだ運賃を回していないのは誰だ？

terms.gloss: The economics faculty, apparently at St Petersburg State University.
terms.why_hard: The colloquial abbreviation should be expanded naturally, and the exact university affiliation should be confirmed from context.

terms.gloss: Crowds of female students described disparagingly as herds.
terms.why_hard: Softening this to groups erases the narrator's detached, objectifying view of the crowd.

terms.gloss: The student elected or appointed to coordinate an academic group and liaise with faculty staff.
terms.why_hard: It is not a class president in the school-age sense, and English and East Asian universities lack a precise equivalent.

terms.gloss: Web-analytics language for traffic, applied metaphorically to the stream of students in the hall.
terms.why_hard: Translating it simply as a crowd loses the deliberate shift into internet-business vocabulary.

terms.gloss: The passing students construed as live, offline user traffic for Durov's website.
terms.why_hard: It must retain both the physical human crowd and the online acquisition metaphor.

terms.gloss: Forming social connections in real life, implicitly contrasted with making them through a social-networking site.
terms.why_hard: A generic make friends may erase the networking vocabulary and the online/offline contrast.

proposed.zh: 在现实生活中建立人际联系
proposed.ja: 現実の生活で人とのつながりを築く

terms.term: «Я знаю, ты здесь. Я знаю, что ты боишься. Боишься нас. Боишься перемен. Я не знаю будущего. Я не могу рассказать тебе, каким оно будет. Но я могу показать тебе, как начать его менять. Я покажу мир без контроля и границ, мир, где возможно все»
terms.gloss: A close adaptation of Neo's closing speech in the 1999 film The Matrix, casting Durov's project as a challenge to control and boundaries.
terms.why_hard: Treating it as original narration misses a major cinematic allusion; the wording should echo each target language's established Matrix translation where possible.

proposed.en: “I know you're there. I know you're afraid. Afraid of us. Afraid of change. I don't know the future. I can't tell you what it will be like. But I can show you how to begin changing it. I will show you a world without control or boundaries, a world where anything is possible.”
proposed.zh: “我知道你在那里。我知道你害怕。害怕我们，害怕改变。我不知道未来会怎样，也无法告诉你未来是什么样子。但我可以让你看到，该如何着手改变它。我会让你看到一个没有控制、没有边界的世界，一个一切皆有可能的世界。”
proposed.ja: 「お前がそこにいることは分かっている。恐れていることも。われわれを、変化を恐れている。未来がどうなるかは分からない。だが、それを変え始める方法なら示せる。支配も境界もない、あらゆることが可能な世界を見せよう」

terms.gloss: Access to the potential user traffic is literally controlled by the building's entrance attendant.
terms.why_hard: The sentence blends web-marketing language with a mundane Soviet-style gatekeeping institution and should preserve both registers.

proposed.en: Access to the traffic is restricted by the gatekeeper
proposed.zh: 这股流量的入口被门卫把着
proposed.ja: そのトラフィックへのアクセスは受付係に制限されている

terms.gloss: An entrance attendant who monitors access to a Russian institutional building and checks identification.
terms.why_hard: Concierge sounds too upscale and security guard too professionalized; the role carries a specifically post-Soviet bureaucratic flavor.

terms.gloss: Durov's student identity card from the philology faculty, which does not authorize entry to the economics building.
terms.why_hard: The abbreviation and faculty affiliation need to remain clear because access depends on institution-specific student credentials.

terms.term: мысленно посылая привет американцам из бара «Идиот»
terms.gloss: Durov silently recalls or mocks Americans encountered at the St Petersburg bar Idiot while using persistent American-style friendliness.
terms.why_hard: The exact earlier anecdote, the bar's identity, and the reason Americans are associated with his repeated smile must be recovered to render the irony accurately.

proposed.en: silently sending his regards to the Americans from the Idiot bar
proposed.zh: 心里向“白痴”酒吧里的那群美国人致意
proposed.ja: 心の中でバー「イディオート」のアメリカ人たちによろしくと伝えながら

terms.gloss: A St Petersburg bar or restaurant named Idiot, after Dostoevsky's novel, known as a haunt for foreign visitors.
terms.why_hard: The name should not be normalized into a generic insult, and its official styling and literary reference require verification.

terms.gloss: Durov presented as an innocuous visitor carrying a small case, with overtones of a salesman or itinerant promoter.
terms.why_hard: The diminutive suggests a modest, nonthreatening case rather than substantial luggage, while the image may deliberately evoke a salesman.

proposed.en: the man with the little case
proposed.zh: 这个拎着小公文包的人
proposed.ja: 小さなかばんを持った男

terms.gloss: The mass protests that followed Russia’s disputed December 2011 parliamentary election.
terms.why_hard: Without context this sounds like generic unrest rather than the politically pivotal 2011–12 election protests.

proposed.ja: 2011年12月の選挙不正に対する抗議運動

terms.gloss: Russia’s centralized state prosecution service, which also exercises broad supervisory powers.
terms.why_hard: It is not equivalent to a local district attorney’s office and carries a stronger implication of state pressure.

terms.gloss: Alexei Navalny, a prominent Russian opposition politician and anti-corruption activist.
terms.why_hard: His political role should be clear without importing knowledge from later stages of his career.

proposed.ja: アレクセイ・ナワリヌイ

terms.gloss: Faust, invoked here as the source of a grandiose Latin maxim about conquering the universe through truth.
terms.why_hard: Readers may assume Goethe’s drama, although the Latin phrase’s attribution and textual origin are disputed.

terms.gloss: A neo-Latin motto conventionally understood as ‘By the power of truth, I, while living, have conquered the universe.’
terms.why_hard: It is a deliberately portentous quotation whose grammar, source, and association with Faust are uncertain.

proposed.en: Vi veri universum vivus vici—“By the power of truth, I, while living, have conquered the universe”
proposed.zh: Vi veri universum vivus vici——“凭借真理的力量，我以生者之身征服了宇宙”
proposed.ja: Vi veri universum vivus vici――「真理の力によって、生けるわれは宇宙を征服した」

terms.gloss: Durov addresses his followers as if broadcasting to a mass-media audience.
terms.why_hard: A flat rendering such as ‘speaks’ loses the comparison between his personal page and a national media outlet.

proposed.ja: ドゥーロフが発信する相手は

terms.gloss: A person given to theatrical, self-important, grandiose gestures.
terms.why_hard: Russian пафосный can mean bombastic or pretentious here, not simply passionate or solemn.

terms.gloss: Entrepreneurs who became millionaires through internet businesses.
terms.why_hard: It does not mean users with a million followers or merely wealthy people who use the internet.

proposed.zh: 靠互联网发家的百万富翁
proposed.ja: インターネット業界で財を成した富豪たち

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the dominant Russian social-networking platform founded by Pavel Durov.
terms.why_hard: Its historical name and capitalization should remain consistent rather than being casually replaced with the later brand VK.

terms.gloss: Copyrighted films uploaded to the platform without the rights holders being notified or authorizing them.
terms.why_hard: The wording euphemistically says ‘without notification,’ while the practical issue is unauthorized or pirated content.

proposed.en: films uploaded without the rights holders’ knowledge or permission
proposed.zh: 未经权利人知情或许可便上传的电影
proposed.ja: 権利者への通知も許諾もなく投稿された映画

terms.gloss: A hall in Moscow’s former Red October chocolate factory complex, later used as an event and technology venue.
terms.why_hard: The text leaves the famous site unnamed; translating it generically loses a recognizable setting in Russia’s new-media scene.

proposed.en: a hall in the former Red October chocolate factory
proposed.zh: 原“红十月”巧克力工厂的一间厂房
proposed.ja: 旧「赤い十月」チョコレート工場のホール

terms.gloss: A Forbes ranking or awards event devoted to entrepreneurs in the internet sector.
terms.why_hard: сетевой here means internet-based, not network-marketing, and the exact Forbes event format may require verification.

proposed.ja: フォーブスのインターネット起業家ランキング

terms.gloss: An award category for the best chief executive officer.
terms.why_hard: The Russian text uses the English corporate acronym, which should not be mistaken for a local title or transliterated as a name.

terms.gloss: Yandex, Russia’s leading search-engine and internet-services company.
terms.why_hard: It should be treated as a company name, not translated literally from its stylized brand.

terms.gloss: Arkady Volozh, a co-founder and then chief executive of Yandex.
terms.why_hard: His title and importance to the Russian internet industry are needed to understand the weight of his vote.

proposed.ja: アルカディ・ヴォロジ

terms.gloss: The emcee colorfully extolled the nominees’ achievements, with mock-heroic overstatement.
terms.why_hard: подвиги literally means heroic feats; rendering it neutrally as ‘achievements’ erases the narrator’s irony.

proposed.en: colorfully recounted the nominees’ heroic exploits
proposed.zh: 绘声绘色地颂扬各位候选人的“丰功伟绩”
proposed.ja: 候補者たちの「英雄的な偉業」を大仰に語り上げた

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte and the book's subject
terms.why_hard: Surname transliteration must stay consistent book-wide (Durov, not 'Duroff')

terms.gloss: Durov's new student forum site, named after St Petersburg State University (SPbGU)
terms.why_hard: A translator might not see it's a domain name punning on the university's Russian acronym; should be kept verbatim, not 'translated'

proposed.zh: spbgu.org（以圣彼得堡大学缩写命名的论坛）

terms.gloss: moderators of the unofficial faculty-level student forums that predated Durov's site
terms.why_hard: These are rival forum admins being co-opted; 'departmental forums' would confuse with official university bodies

proposed.ja: 学部フォーラムの管理人たち

terms.gloss: the 1999 film The Matrix; the green falling code is its visual signature
terms.why_hard: Title localization differs by market and must match the local official release title

terms.gloss: the green cascading binary/hex code imagery from The Matrix
terms.why_hard: 'Binary' is technically inaccurate to the film (it's stylized glyphs), but must render the allusion

terms.term: «Пора неграм отплатить Америке за 310 лет рабства»
terms.gloss: voice-over of Durov's provocative recruitment poster mimicking Black revolutionary rhetoric (310 years ≈ slavery era since 1619)
terms.why_hard: This is Durov's own deliberately transgressive pastiche; a translator must keep the borrowed militant register without adding disclaimers or flattening it, and keep the number as written

proposed.en: "It's time for negroes to pay America back for 310 years of slavery"
proposed.zh: 「是时候让黑人向美国讨还310年奴隶制的血债了」
proposed.ja: 「黒人はアメリカに310年間の奴隷制の借りを返す時が来た」

terms.gloss: revolution as the recurring metaphor for Durov's campus forum takeover
terms.why_hard: Tone must stay mock-heroic throughout; 'uprising', 'revolt' and 'revolution' drift apart across the book

terms.term: враг, который у нас один на всех
terms.gloss: the single common enemy of all students — implicitly the existing forum powers / official university sites
terms.why_hard: Deliberately vague propaganda idiom; keeping the vagueness is the point

terms.gloss: Durov's earlier forum site (spelled with Russian 'с' in the source text)
terms.why_hard: Must stay as a verbatim URL; some editions show a Cyrillic 'с' as a typo — normalize, don't translate

terms.gloss: 2000s Russian internet slang for 'users'
terms.why_hard: Period slang; rendering as neutral 'users' loses the dated internet-culture flavor

terms.gloss: 'this thing will turn university life upside down' — Durov's grandiose internal voice
terms.why_hard: Register decision: comic hyperbole vs. sincere boast; must match the narrator's ironic distance

proposed.en: This thing is going to turn university life upside down
proposed.zh: 这东西将彻底改变大学的生态
proposed.ja: これは大学生活を一変させる

terms.gloss: 'freedom' — Durov's lifelong brand word, first deployed as forum marketing
terms.why_hard: The book's central recurring keyword; must be the same word every time (自由 in zh/ja) to track the through-line from forum to VK to Telegram

terms.gloss: a banner/graphic badge reading 'No ads!' on the forum page
terms.why_hard: 'Плашка' is web-design jargon for a graphic label; 'plaque' or 'plate' would be wrong

terms.gloss: marketers — stock villains of Durov's ideology from the start
terms.why_hard: Recurring pejorative class in the book; 'marketeers/marketers' choice set here propagates

terms.gloss: 'metastases of the consumer society' — cancer imagery for advertising culture
terms.why_hard: Medical metaphor must stay a medical metaphor; 'spread of consumerism' would lose the malignancy note

proposed.en: The metastases of the consumer society

terms.gloss: 'enslaving everyone who thinks in stereotypes' — links back to the slavery poster language
terms.why_hard: Echoes 'рабство' deliberately; the zh/ja rendering should reuse the same slavery word as the poster

proposed.en: enslaving anyone who thinks in clichés
proposed.zh: 奴役着一切按刻板印象思考的人
proposed.ja: ステレオタイプでしか考えられない者を奴隷化する

terms.gloss: an anime-style girl — Durov putting manga/anime-style pinup art on the site header
terms.why_hard: Requires knowing mid-2000s Russian internet culture, where anime art on forums was a standard traffic draw; 'cartoon girl' would flatten it

terms.term: приоткрываем ей декольте, подчеркиваем талию, бедра
terms.gloss: designer's directions on the pinup art: slightly open neckline, emphasized waist, hips
terms.why_hard: Present-tense work-in-progress narration; a translator might turn it into description and lose the Photoshop-monologue effect

proposed.en: we give her a slightly open neckline, emphasize her waist, her hips
proposed.zh: 微敞她的领口，突出腰线和臀部
proposed.ja: 胸元を少し開かせ、ウエストとヒップを強調する

terms.gloss: to troll — attack/provoke someone online
terms.why_hard: 2000s verb already established; 'mock' or 'tease' would under-translate; zh has no settled verb, so pick one and hold it

terms.gloss: lofty spiritual-mindedness — what a troll target gets mocked for
terms.why_hard: Ironically inflated abstraction; 'spirituality' alone is wrong — it's pretentious high-mindedness

terms.term: Пафос не должен отрываться от земли
terms.gloss: 'the pathos must not detach from the ground' — grand rhetoric must stay anchored to base instincts
terms.why_hard: 'Пафос' here means grandiose rhetoric (not 'pathos' in English); whole sentence is Durov's cynical design maxim

proposed.en: Grand rhetoric must keep its feet on the ground
proposed.zh: 豪言壮语不能脱离地面
proposed.ja: 大仰な主張は地に足をつけねばならない

terms.gloss: 'to land a visual strike' — make a splash with eye-catching graphics
terms.why_hard: Military metaphor in marketing context; must keep the mock-combat tone Durov frames everything in

proposed.ja: ビジュアル面で一撃を加える

terms.term: вручить власть тем, у кого ее нет и кто ее хочет
terms.gloss: 'to hand power to those who don't have it and want it' — Durov's tactic of empowering the discontented
terms.why_hard: Sounds like a political slogan; the ambiguity (marketing trick vs. sincere creed) must be preserved

proposed.en: to hand power to those who don't have it and want it
proposed.zh: 把权力交给那些没有权力却渴望权力的人
proposed.ja: 権力を持たず、それを欲する者たちに権力を渡す

terms.gloss: colloquial 'to flap one's tongue' — talk uselessly
terms.why_hard: Register: colloquial dismissive idiom inside the poster's militant rhetoric; must not become formal 'empty talk'

proposed.ja: 口先だけならもうたくさんだ

terms.gloss: posters promoting the forum, styled like revolutionary recruitment posters
terms.why_hard: 'Афиша' is a public poster/flyer (event publicity), not 'poster' in the decorative sense

proposed.ja: フォーラムのポスター

terms.gloss: light yellow-green (salad green), distinct from 'зеленый' green
terms.why_hard: Russian distinguishes two greens; most languages have one word and need a modifier to keep the pair

terms.gloss: Classmate who, with Paperno, led the class’s mock-state game
terms.why_hard: Unfamiliar proper name; must stay consistent if he reappears later

terms.gloss: Classmate co-leader of the mock constitution/democracy game
terms.why_hard: Jewish/Russian surname with several possible Latinizations

terms.gloss: Roof of a bunker by an airfield where Durov read
terms.why_hard: Unclear if a real St Petersburg school/airfield landmark or a local nickname

proposed.en: the bunker roof by the airfield
proposed.ja: 飛行場そばの掩体壕の屋上

terms.gloss: Carlos Castaneda, New Age/anthropology cult author popular with teens
terms.why_hard: Russian uses surname only; English readers need Carlos, Chinese/Japanese need established book-market forms

terms.gloss: Napoleon Hill, U.S. self-help author of Think and Grow Rich
terms.why_hard: Must match the standard local spelling of the self-help brand, not a calque

terms.term: «Ты – то, что ты думаешь; думай и богатей»
terms.gloss: Mash-up of Hill’s slogan and the Russian title of Think and Grow Rich
terms.why_hard: Looks like a quote but is two fused self-help tags; translating literally loses the book title

proposed.en: “You are what you think; think and grow rich.”
proposed.ja: 「思考は現実化する。考えよ、さらば富まん」

terms.gloss: Goncharov’s novel Oblomov, set text in Russian schools
terms.why_hard: Must use the canonical local title of the novel, not a new transliteration

terms.gloss: Ilya Ilyich Oblomov, the idle gentleman protagonist
terms.why_hard: Patronymic form; dropping it loses the schoolroom register, translating it sounds odd

terms.gloss: Stock classroom cliché: Oblomov as ‘mirror of the Russian soul’
terms.why_hard: Literal ‘mirror’ is fine but the phrase is a frozen school essay formula

proposed.en: a mirror of the Russian soul

terms.gloss: Andrei Stolz, Oblomov’s half-German, industrious foil
terms.why_hard: German name via Russian; Stolz vs Shtolts vs Stolz must be locked

terms.gloss: Pejorative, folksy slur for a German / German-like person
terms.why_hard: Stronger and ruder than ‘German’; sanitizing it flattens the class’s Slavophile take

terms.gloss: School literature teacher who favored medieval/troubadour texts
terms.why_hard: Real or composite name that must not be respelt later

terms.gloss: Teacher of Russian language and literature (slovesnost’)
terms.why_hard: Not simply ‘literature’; slovesnost’ is the old gymnasium subject name

terms.gloss: Durov tagged as ‘the Italian’ (family lore of Italian ancestry)
terms.why_hard: Looks like a nationality slip; it is an epithet, not a fact error

proposed.ja: イタリア人のドゥロフ

terms.gloss: Provençal and Lombard troubadours, Guskov’s obscure medieval focus
terms.why_hard: Provençal vs Occitan, Lombard vs Lombardy; specialist terms with standard forms

proposed.zh: 普罗旺斯或伦巴第行吟诗人
proposed.ja: プロヴァンスやロンバルディアのトルバドゥール

terms.gloss: Idée fixe; Durov’s compulsion to oppose the consensus
terms.why_hard: French via Russian; keep as loan or flatten to ‘obsession’

proposed.ja: 固定観念（イデー・フィクス）

terms.gloss: English loan in the Russian text: someone who takes the opposite view
terms.why_hard: Already English in source; zh/ja need a business-bio equivalent, not a re-loan dump

terms.gloss: Narrator’s aside: irony that a ‘noble’ Russian surname speaks against Oblomov
terms.why_hard: Vocative interjection, not a sentence; over-explaining kills the wink

proposed.ja: ああ、ロシア貴族の姓よ！

terms.gloss: Work that romanticizes laziness (Durov’s charge against Oblomov)
terms.why_hard: ‘Poeticize’ vs ‘glorify’ vs ‘romanticize’ changes how harsh the student sounds

terms.gloss: Pavel's older half-brother Mikhail, already adult and living apart from their mother
terms.why_hard: Must stay distinct from Nikolai and Pavel; 'сводный' means half-brother, not stepbrother

terms.gloss: half-sibling (same mother, different father in this family context)
terms.why_hard: English 'stepbrother' is wrong; Chinese/Japanese kinship terms split half vs step

terms.gloss: Pavel's middle brother Nikolai Durov, the mathematical prodigy
terms.why_hard: Later a major VK/Telegram figure; name must match the rest of the book (Nikolai not Nicholas)

terms.gloss: the airfield Pavel wanted to visit; Nikolai was too cerebral to care
terms.why_hard: Could be misread as airport (аэропорт) rather than a working airfield

terms.gloss: a popular-science astronomy book given to three-year-old Nikolai on a trolleybus
terms.why_hard: Likely Flammarion or a Soviet Popular Astronomy; title should look like a real book, not a generic phrase

terms.gloss: Soviet/Russian trolleybus, the setting of the reading anecdote
terms.why_hard: Not a bus or tram; the vehicle type is part of the period texture

terms.gloss: cubic equations Nikolai could solve at age seven
terms.why_hard: Must not become 'cube roots' or 'quadratic'; signals genuine math prodigy

terms.gloss: a TV talent/prodigy show Nikolai was invited onto
terms.why_hard: 'Wunderkind' is German loan in Russian; calquing vs local analogue (春晚神童, 神童番組) is a register choice

terms.gloss: the family's move from the Baltic (St Petersburg) to the Adriatic (Italy)
terms.why_hard: Seas as synecdoche for cities/countries; 'Baltic to Adriatic' must stay geographic, not brand-like

proposed.en: from the Baltic to the Adriatic
proposed.zh: 从波罗的海迁到亚得里亚海
proposed.ja: バルト海からアドリア海へ

terms.gloss: the father's Soviet/Russian kandidat/doktor of philology, offered a post teaching Russian abroad
terms.why_hard: 'Doctor of philology' is not a US PhD in linguistics; over-translating as PhD flattens the Soviet degree

terms.gloss: the Italian host: head of an Institute of Russian Language awaited in Turin
terms.why_hard: Could be confused with Moscow's Vinogradov Institute; here it is the Italian posting

terms.gloss: Turin, Italy, where the one-room apartment awaited
terms.why_hard: Russian Турин is Turin, not Tours; keep the Italian city consistent

terms.gloss: the father as a Latinist (classicist), the rhetorical question of India vs Italy
terms.why_hard: Not 'Latin Americanist'; means scholar of Latin language/literature

terms.gloss: epithet for little Pavel, the boy associated with Cervantes (left behind in Petersburg)
terms.why_hard: Quoted nickname; must not be unpacked into a plot summary or dropped as obscure

proposed.ja: 「セルバンテスを抱えた少年」

terms.gloss: Nevsky Prospect, St Petersburg's main avenue, where the grandmother's room was
terms.why_hard: Must match book's spelling of the avenue everywhere (Nevsky Prospect vs Prospekt vs Avenue)

terms.gloss: kommunalka: shared Soviet communal apartment whose other rooms surround the grandmother's 30 m²
terms.why_hard: Not 'apartment building' or 'dorm'; the communal-flat purgatory is the point

terms.gloss: the rest of the kommunalka as a 'purgatory' encircling her room
terms.why_hard: Catholic purgatory image in a Soviet flat; 'hell' overstates, 'hallway' understates

proposed.en: the purgatory of the communal flat

terms.gloss: habit from the Leningrad Blockade: hoarding and canning vast amounts of food
terms.why_hard: блокада is the 1941–44 siege, not a generic blockade; losing that loses the grandmother's psychology

proposed.zh: 列宁格勒围城留下的习惯
proposed.ja: レニングラード封鎖時代の癖

terms.gloss: four-year-old Pavel smashing the grandmother's jars as 'jars of betrayal' when told he is being left behind
terms.why_hard: банки are canning jars, not banks; предательства is figurative, not a brand of preserves

proposed.ja: 裏切りの瓶を叩き割る

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the founder of the student forum spbgu.org and later VKontakte.
terms.why_hard: His surname should follow the biography’s established transliteration and naming convention.

terms.gloss: A rival forum participant whom Durov sought to humiliate and deprive of female admiration.
terms.why_hard: His identity and any established nickname or transliteration cannot be inferred from this passage alone.

terms.gloss: Durov’s capitalized online epithet or persona, literally “the Architect.”
terms.why_hard: Lowercasing it or translating it descriptively would obscure that it functions as a recurring title or handle.

terms.gloss: An old, sexist euphemism for women, literally “the weaker sex.”
terms.why_hard: A neutral translation such as “women” would erase the period’s patronizing and ironic register.

terms.gloss: A secondary or disguised online account used to speak or attack under another identity.
terms.why_hard: It does not mean a generic virtual entity here but an alt account or sockpuppet in Russian forum slang.

terms.gloss: The name of the online persona or alternate account used to attack Innokenty in comments.
terms.why_hard: The handle should remain stable, while research may reveal who controlled it and whether its capitalization was stylized.

terms.gloss: A quoted label for a Durov-aligned clique on the forum that attracted intense admiration.
terms.why_hard: It may be a formal group name rather than merely a figurative reference to a clique.

terms.gloss: The ability of attractive and socially active female users to draw men and energize an online community.
terms.why_hard: The English slogan is used with an instrumental, somewhat cynical meaning rather than its usual feminist sense.

terms.gloss: Colloquial shorthand for Kazan Cathedral in central St Petersburg.
terms.why_hard: A literal adjective such as “Kazan” leaves the landmark unidentified for readers without local knowledge.

terms.gloss: Durov’s student-oriented online forum associated with St Petersburg State University.
terms.why_hard: It must be distinguished consistently from the university itself and from Durov’s later social network VKontakte.

terms.gloss: Software or website features, expressed in Russian internet-industry jargon borrowed from English.
terms.why_hard: An overly formal equivalent would lose Durov’s casual product-development register.

terms.gloss: Users who generate interaction and organize other people around the content they create.
terms.why_hard: This is a managerial coinage, not a standard job title such as content manager or event organizer.

proposed.ja: コンテンツのオーガナイザー

terms.gloss: Exceptionally driven and socially energetic, echoing Lev Gumilev’s theory of passionarity.
terms.why_hard: Rendering it merely as “passionate” misses a recognizable Russian intellectual buzzword about history-shaping energy.

terms.gloss: Deliberately becoming friendly with someone, with an informal suggestion of cultivating a social connection.
terms.why_hard: A plain “making friends” can miss the strategic and colloquial overtones of the Russian verb.

proposed.ja: 彼女たちと親しくなり

terms.gloss: The forum understood as Durov’s own online venue or platform competing for users.
terms.why_hard: The literal meaning is a physical site, while recurring internet usage requires a consistent platform metaphor.

terms.gloss: A symbolic figure or emblem around which the forum community formed, likely referring to Durov or his online persona.
terms.why_hard: The referent is unstated here, so translating it too concretely could misidentify a recurring symbol or person.

terms.gloss: Durov's university classmate and later close friend, a recurring first-hand witness in the book
terms.why_hard: Recurring named source; his surname must be transliterated and kept identical throughout the book

terms.gloss: Faculty of Oriental Studies at St Petersburg State University
terms.why_hard: A clipped Russian faculty name that cannot be calqued literally; needs full expansion on first use

terms.gloss: Philology Faculty of St Petersburg State University, where Durov studied
terms.why_hard: Same clipping problem; must stay consistent with how Durov's own faculty is named across all segments

terms.gloss: Alexander Kazem-Bek, first dean of the Oriental faculty, a famous 19th-century orientalist
terms.why_hard: A historical figure whose bust stands in the hall; translator must not mangle the hyphenated Persian-origin surname

proposed.ja: アレクサンドル・カゼム＝ベク

terms.gloss: Jan Baudouin de Courtenay, first dean of the philology faculty, major linguist
terms.why_hard: Polish-French surname with established Western spellings that differ from the Russian graphemes

proposed.ja: ボドゥアン・ド・クルトネ

terms.gloss: Widely known nickname of philology faculties — mostly female students, jokingly seen as a place to find a wife
terms.why_hard: A Russian in-joke; a literal 'faculty of brides' reads bizarre without a nudge that it is a folk nickname

proposed.en: the 'bride faculty', as philology was nicknamed for its abundance of girls
proposed.zh: "出新娘的系"（语文系女生多的绰号）
proposed.ja: 「花嫁学部」（女子が多いことから付けられた文学部の俗称）

terms.gloss: 2010s slang for a rich kid / spoiled child of wealthy parents
terms.why_hard: False friend of English 'major'; the class connotation must be preserved, not the word shape

proposed.ja: 御曹司・金持ちの息子

terms.gloss: A wild card — someone without a fixed type, an unpredictable live wire
terms.why_hard: Card-game image; must keep the 'unreadable, anything-can-happen' sense rather than 'joker' as clown

proposed.ja: ジョーカーのような存在

terms.term: анекдот про разницу между программистом-интровертом и программистом-экстравертом
terms.gloss: Classic programmer joke: the introvert looks at his own shoes, the extrovert at yours
terms.why_hard: The punchline is implied, not quoted; translator must supply the shoes/shoes structure or the sentence collapses

proposed.en: the joke about the difference between an introverted and an extroverted programmer (one stares at his own shoes, the other at yours)
proposed.zh: 关于内向程序员和外向程序员差别的段子（一个盯着自己的鞋，一个盯着你的鞋）
proposed.ja: 内向的なプログラマーと外向的なプログラマーの違いを語る有名なジョーク（前者は自分の靴、後者は相手の靴を見る）

terms.gloss: Elevated/quasi-biblical enumerative idiom for 'a huge number', applied ironically to pretty girls
terms.why_hard: A deliberately literary flourish a plain rendering like 'lots' would flatten; register matters

proposed.en: a whole swarm, a host, a flock of lovely girls
proposed.zh: 一大群、一大片、成群结队的漂亮姑娘
proposed.ja: うじゃうじゃと、雲霞のごとく群れをなす美しい娘たち

terms.gloss: Colloquial 'yammered / chattered non-stop'
terms.why_hard: Marked colloquial verb inside narration; a neutral 'talked' loses the comic breathlessness

terms.gloss: The non-specialised, ordinary-stream classes at Durov's elite St Petersburg school, contrasted with advanced tracks
terms.why_hard: Implies the school had elite tracks Durov was not in; needs the school system context to avoid confusion

proposed.ja: 普通クラス（特進クラスではない）

terms.gloss: Palace Bridge across the Neva, between Vasilievsky Island (university) and the city center
terms.why_hard: Standard St Petersburg toponym; must match the book's naming of all bridges

proposed.ja: 宮殿橋（ドヴォルツォーヴイ橋）

terms.gloss: Nevsky Prospekt metro station, near the philology faculty on Vosstaniya square side
terms.why_hard: Station names are quoted in Russian; target-language metro conventions differ

terms.term: город хоккея и едкого дыма из труб
terms.gloss: Periphrasis for the narrator's/Perекopsky's industrial home city (smokestacks plus a famous hockey team)
terms.why_hard: The city is never named; translator must identify it from earlier segments and keep the periphrasis or the reader loses the referent

proposed.en: a town of hockey and acrid chimney smoke
proposed.zh: 那座以冰球和烟囱呛人浓烟闻名的城市
proposed.ja: アイスホッケーと煙突の辛い煙の街

terms.gloss: The small two-storey 18th-century mansion housing the philology faculty at 11 Sredny Prospekt, Vasilievsky Island
terms.why_hard: 'Usadba' here is a cramped town house, not a country estate; a wrong choice suggests a rural manor

proposed.en: the two-storey mansion that housed the faculty
proposed.zh: 语文系所在的两层小楼
proposed.ja: 学部が入居する二階建ての館

terms.gloss: A light 'burn' — the shared tingling thrill of possibility at the start of university life
terms.why_hard: Sensory image tied to the book's fire/tingling motif for Durov's charisma; needs one consistent rendering across chapters

terms.gloss: Short for 'expatriate' — a foreign businessman working in Russia; here a Western payment-company representative.
terms.why_hard: Translating as 'expatriate' or 'foreigner' loses the period business-slang flavor of 'экспат' in 2000s Moscow/St Petersburg offices.

terms.gloss: Narrator's epithet for the VK side's negotiator in the bargaining scene.
terms.why_hard: If rendered variously ('negotiator', 'interlocutor', 'the man'), the recurring epithet that keeps the scene faceless and bureaucratic is lost.

terms.gloss: A silent coder present at the meeting, typing at a keyboard throughout.
terms.why_hard: Easy to conflate with the negotiator; must stay distinct as a separate character.

terms.gloss: An unnamed, eccentric figure in a baseball cap — almost certainly Pavel Durov, kept anonymous for comic effect.
terms.why_hard: Rendering 'тип' neutrally ('man in a cap') loses the dismissive slang; translators must keep the anonymous epithet even though readers will guess who it is.

proposed.en: the guy in the baseball cap

terms.gloss: VK's 'Wishes/Gifts' service (подарки/приложения) letting users give virtual gifts to friends — actually the VK gift app in the negotiation.
terms.why_hard: A literal 'Desires' translation is wrong; this is a product name and should be traced to the real VK feature.

terms.gloss: VK's internal currency ('votes', голоса) used to buy gifts.
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent with how 'голоса/votes' are rendered elsewhere in the book; 'our currency' alone obscures the in-app payments system.

terms.gloss: Inventory turnover — the expat's business jargon for why different goods merit different percentages.
terms.why_hard: Retail/finance jargon; 'rotation' or 'circulation' would be wrong.

terms.gloss: Stock phrase 'it's just business, nothing personal'.
terms.why_hard: An idiomatic set phrase; must match the standard rendering used across the book.

proposed.ja: ビジネスであって、個人的な感情ではない

terms.gloss: 'Reinforced-concrete' firm conviction — Soviet-era slang for an unshakeable belief.
terms.why_hard: The concrete metaphor reads oddly literally; needs a natural strength idiom in each language, consistently.

proposed.en: had learned, hard as reinforced concrete,
proposed.ja: 鉄筋コンクリートのように固く心得ていた

terms.gloss: 'Everything has its price' — the expat's cynical creed.
terms.why_hard: Must stay a recurring creed-phrase, not paraphrased each time.

proposed.ja: すべてには値段がつく

terms.term: благородные устремления существуют, чтобы набить цену
terms.gloss: Noble aspirations exist only to inflate the asking price (in bargaining).
terms.why_hard: 'Набить цену' is market-stall idiom (to talk up the price); literal translation garbles the sarcasm.

proposed.en: noble aspirations exist to talk up the price
proposed.zh: 高尚的抱负不过是为了抬价
proposed.ja: 崇高な理想とは値段を吊り上げるためだけのもの

terms.gloss: 'The guys are just haggling' — expat's dismissive read of VK's behavior.
terms.why_hard: 'Парни' (the guys/lads) must match the book's broader rendering of the VK founders' casual in-group.

proposed.zh: 这些人不过是在讨价还价。
proposed.ja: 連中はただ値切っているだけだ

terms.gloss: Soft/plush toys — a gift category in the VK gift shop.
terms.why_hard: Trivial but part of a recurring gift taxonomy; must match other segments' category names.

terms.gloss: The commission percentage VK demands on sales — 10% demanded, doubled to 20% as an ultimatum.
terms.why_hard: Percent-vs-percentage-points and consistency of 'комиссия' (commission) throughout the negotiation arc.

proposed.ja: 10パーセント／20パーセントの手数料

terms.term: кнопка, которая в один клик позволяет приобрести подарок
terms.gloss: The one-click buy button VK offers the merchant inside its service.
terms.why_hard: 'В один клик' is the fixed web phrase 'in one click'; must match other e-commerce references in the book.

proposed.en: a one-click button to buy the gift
proposed.ja: ワンクリックでギフトを購入できるボタン

terms.gloss: Fidgeting/squirming in his chair — the expat's discomfort.
terms.why_hard: Minor, but body-language verbs recur in character sketches and should be kept natural, not literal.

proposed.ja: 椅子の上でそわそわと体を動かしながら

terms.gloss: Skeptical turn/shake of the head by the programmer, without stopping typing.
terms.why_hard: Ambiguous gesture (shake vs. look around); 'покрутил' implies dismissive rotation of the head.

terms.gloss: Suddenly bellowed — the baseball-cap figure's explosive outburst.
terms.why_hard: 'Заорал' is more violent than 'shouted'; register of the Durov outburst matters for the character portrait.

terms.term: сунул руки в карманы черных брюк
terms.gloss: Hands in pockets of black trousers — part of Durov's trademark all-black dress.
terms.why_hard: The black clothing is a recurring Durov signifier across segments; 'black trousers' must be kept, not generalized.

proposed.en: thrust his hands into the pockets of his black trousers
proposed.zh: 双手插进黑色长裤的口袋
proposed.ja: 黒いズボンのポケットに両手を突っ込んだ

terms.gloss: Slightly lopsided, leaning forward — Durov's odd gait.
terms.why_hard: 'Скособочившись' is colloquial and physical; a literal 'bent sideways' sounds clinical rather than wry.

proposed.ja: 少し体を斜めに前かがみになりながら

terms.gloss: 'This figure's eccentricity' — ironic epithet ('деятель', a mildly contemptuous 'operator/character').
terms.why_hard: 'Деятель' carries Soviet-era sarcastic connotation of a self-important operator; neutral 'person' loses the irony.

proposed.ja: この人物の風変わりな振る舞い

terms.gloss: Free indirect thought of the expat: 'we're all respectable people here' — his shock at the outburst.
terms.why_hard: Sarcastic interior monologue; must be kept as deadpan, not turned into a quoted line.

proposed.zh: 我们这儿可都是体面人
proposed.ja: ここにいるのは皆まともな大人のはずだ

terms.gloss: The foreigner (same expat) — shift of epithet signaling the narrative viewpoint.
terms.why_hard: Epithet switching (экспат/иностранец/менеджер) for the same person must be tracked so translation doesn't invent two characters.

terms.gloss: Yet another epithet for the expat, from his own professional self-image.
terms.why_hard: Must be recognized as the same character; 'manager' vs 'the expat' consistency question for the whole scene.

terms.term: разный процент с разных категорий товара
terms.gloss: Tiered commission by product category — the deal structure at stake.
terms.why_hard: Legal/commerce phrasing; 'процент' here means commission rate, not simple percentage, and recurs in the whole negotiation arc.

proposed.en: a different commission rate for each product category
proposed.zh: 不同商品类别适用不同抽成比例
proposed.ja: 商品カテゴリーごとに異なる手数料率

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the dominant Russian social network founded by Pavel Durov
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render it as 'In Contact' or leave it transliterated inconsistently; the book uses it constantly and the name must be fixed early

terms.gloss: Afisha, a Moscow-based culture and lifestyle magazine (1999–2015) that was the voice of urban Russian hipsters
terms.why_hard: Without knowing the magazine's cultural weight, a translator might render it as a generic 'magazine' or miss the ironic citation tone

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, the book's subject
terms.why_hard: Name must be consistent across the whole book; patronymic and diminutives may appear later

proposed.ja: パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ

terms.gloss: Nikolai Kononov, the author of this biography (Код Дурова)
terms.why_hard: He is referred to by surname only here; a translator unfamiliar with the book's authorship might not realize this is the author himself being referenced in the third person

terms.gloss: A Hero of Our Time, the 1840 Lermontov novel; here used as a high-literary label for a 'defining figure of the era'
terms.why_hard: Capitalization signals the allusion; a translator who treats it as a plain phrase loses the ironic literary echo

terms.gloss: 'Digital elite' — the small caste of tech entrepreneurs who rose to wealth and power
terms.why_hard: The scare quotes in Russian signal distance/irony; dropping them flattens the author's skeptical tone

terms.gloss: 'Hordes of mini-Durovs' — a hyperbolic image of future clone-entrepreneurs
terms.why_hard: полчища carries a slightly pejorative/military connotation (like 'hordes'); a neutral 'army' or 'legions' would soften the irony

proposed.ja: ミニ・ドゥーロフの群れ

terms.gloss: 'Think globally, act locally' — a well-known slogan, here repurposed for tech entrepreneurship
terms.why_hard: This is a recognized English-language slogan; a translator should use the established equivalent rather than a literal re-translation

proposed.ja: グローバルに考え、ローカルに動く

terms.gloss: 'Far-Reaching Conclusions' — capitalized for ironic emphasis, mocking grand generalizations
terms.why_hard: The capitalization is a stylistic device signalling sarcasm; a translator who lowercases it loses the author's distancing

terms.term: Как Все В Мире Будет Устроено
terms.gloss: 'How Everything in the World Will Be Arranged' — another capitalized ironic phrase mocking utopian futurology
terms.why_hard: Same capitalization-as-irony device as above; must be rendered with equivalent typographic or rhetorical marking in each target language

proposed.en: How Everything in the World Will Work

terms.gloss: 'Dragged into his nets' — a predatory/fishing metaphor for user acquisition
terms.why_hard: The verb затащил is colloquial and slightly aggressive ('dragged in'); a neutral 'attracted' would lose the implied manipulation

proposed.ja: 自らの網に引き込んだ

terms.gloss: 'Stirs the imagination' — a set phrase implying fascination mixed with unease
terms.why_hard: будоражить has a slightly agitating, unsettling nuance beyond simple 'inspire'; a flat 'captures the imagination' misses the ambivalence

terms.gloss: Gopniki — aggressive street toughs, typically from working-class housing estates, associated with tracksuits, squatting, and petty crime
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render as 'thugs' or 'hooligans' and lose the specific post-Soviet housing-estate connotation that is essential to the setting

terms.gloss: Sitsevaya Street — a street name in the Kamenskaya/Kupchino area of St Petersburg, used here as a nickname for a housing cluster
terms.why_hard: A translator might try to translate the meaning of the adjective ('calico') rather than keeping it as a proper name

terms.gloss: Kamyshovaya Street — a street name in the same district, used here as a nickname for a neighboring housing cluster
terms.why_hard: Same issue as Sitsevaya; 'kamysh' means reeds, and the translator must decide whether to transliterate or translate the street name

terms.gloss: Cities beyond the Arctic Circle — Soviet-era settlements like Norilsk or Vorkuta where construction was limited to hilltops due to permafrost
terms.why_hard: A translator might simply say 'Arctic cities' and miss the specific Soviet industrial-town connotation of isolation and brutal planning

terms.gloss: Hills or hillocks, specifically the low rounded hills characteristic of northern and Far Eastern Russian terrain
terms.why_hard: A translator might use 'mountains' or 'hills' generically; the word carries a specific geographical register tied to northern Russia and Siberia

terms.gloss: Mixed wild grasses and herbs — a botanical/geographical term for the diverse herbaceous vegetation of meadows
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might say 'weeds' or 'wildflowers'; the term is a specific Russian ecological concept implying rich, varied grassland

terms.gloss: Stylobate — the raised platform or base level of a building, here the ground-floor commercial podium common in modern Russian apartment blocks
terms.why_hard: An architectural term that most English readers won't recognize; a translator must decide whether to keep the technical term or paraphrase as 'podium' or 'base'

terms.gloss: Squandered or embezzled the money — colloquial for losing or stealing construction funds
terms.why_hard: The verb 'просадить' is informal and implies reckless loss; a neutral translation like 'the money was spent' would lose the connotation of corruption or waste

terms.gloss: Excavation pits — large open holes dug for building foundations, common on abandoned construction sites
terms.why_hard: Might be rendered simply as 'pits' or 'holes'; the word specifically means foundation excavation pits, evoking unfinished Soviet/post-Soviet construction

terms.gloss: Giant prefabricated apartment blocks — the standard Soviet panel housing (panelki) personified as towering giants looking down on workers
terms.why_hard: The personification and the specific reference to panel construction (panelki) must both survive; 'giants' alone loses the housing type, and 'apartment buildings' alone loses the literary effect

proposed.ja: パネル工法の巨大な集合住宅

terms.gloss: A new metro station, the last on the line — almost certainly the long-delayed stations of the St Petersburg Metro's Frunzensky radius (e.g., Volkovskaya or later stations), notorious for construction delays
terms.why_hard: A translator unaware of St Petersburg's metro history would miss the irony of 'expectations stretching on for years'; this is a pointed local reference, not a generic detail

proposed.en: a new station, the last on the line

terms.gloss: Peat — the area around St Petersburg was historically marshland where peat was harvested and transported, explaining the drained swamps mentioned earlier
terms.why_hard: A translator might not connect the peat road to the drained swamps and the overall landscape description, losing the coherence of the passage's geography

terms.gloss: Espionage-style stunts (infiltrating faculties to gather content or provoke interest)
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render it as literal spy stories rather than framing it as a metaphor for guerrilla marketing tactics

terms.gloss: Abbreviation for исторический факультет (History Faculty) at a Russian university
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might leave it untranslated or render it as a proper noun without clarifying it's a faculty abbreviation

terms.gloss: The average/typical student; a set phrase in Russian journalistic prose
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might over-literalize as 'statistically average student' instead of the natural equivalent

terms.gloss: Colloquial verb for browsing the internet (лазать = to crawl/climb, used informally for surfing online)
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might use a formal register like 'accessed the internet' and lose the casual 2000s tone

terms.gloss: Catalyst — used metaphorically for an offline event that would drive people online
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might keep the chemistry metaphor too literally; it needs to read as a strategic concept

terms.gloss: The Kremlin clock (chimes) on the Spasskaya Tower, iconic symbol of New Year in Russia
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might just say 'the clock on the tower' without evoking the Kremlin chimes tradition; the reader needs to feel the New Year countdown

proposed.en: The Kremlin chimes on the tower
proposed.zh: 克里姆林宫塔楼上的钟声

terms.gloss: The ruby stars atop the Kremlin towers, Soviet symbols still in place in 2004
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might not convey that these are the famous Soviet-era red stars on Kremlin spires, or might miss the ironic tone of 'didn't bother to remove'

terms.gloss: Demiurge — used ironically/grandly to refer to Zuckerberg as the creator of his world (Facebook)
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might use 'creator' and lose the mythological grandeur and slight irony of the Russian

terms.gloss: Internet nerd/geek — задрот is a derogatory slang term for an obsessive nerd, here used self-deprecatingly
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might use a neutral word like 'user' or 'enthusiast' and lose the dismissive connotation that makes the transformation dramatic

terms.gloss: Hacked a server — informal borrowing from English, standard in Russian tech/internet slang of the 2000s
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might over-formalize or miss that this is casual register matching the era's hacker culture

proposed.ja: サーバーをハッキングした

terms.gloss: Downloaded/scraped files — выкачать literally means 'to pump out', colloquial for mass-downloading
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might say 'downloaded files' without conveying the bulk, somewhat illicit extraction implied

proposed.ja: ファイルを吸い出した

terms.gloss: To promote oneself / gain traction — colloquial term for self-promotion or building buzz
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might use a formal business term like 'market himself' and lose the informal entrepreneurial energy

terms.gloss: Military metaphor: preparatory bombardment before an offensive; here the PR buildup before the contest finale.
terms.why_hard: Literal 'artillery preparation' is opaque; needs a punchy military image consistent with the book's war framing of Durov's stunts.

terms.gloss: 'Miss Audience Sympathies' — the viewer's-choice title awarded by student votes in Soviet/post-Soviet beauty contests.
terms.why_hard: A fixed contest formula; must be rendered as a recurring title, not paraphrased each time.

terms.gloss: Mark Zuckerberg, founder of Facebook, whose Facemash stunt Durov's contest echoes.
terms.why_hard: The allusion to Facemash (rating girls' photos) only lands if the name is the standard transliteration in each language.

terms.gloss: A deliberately provocative 'bomb' of a scandal, referring to Facemash.
terms.why_hard: Reader must connect to the earlier Facemash episode; the scandal-blast sense, not a literal device.

terms.gloss: Downscaling metaphor: if Zuckerberg's stunt was a bomb, this was a grenade that still exploded before the final.
terms.why_hard: The bomb/grenade scale contrast must be kept so the comparison reads as calibration, not separate images.

proposed.en: a grenade that still went off right before the final
proposed.zh: 一枚照样在决赛前爆炸的手榴弹
proposed.ja: それでも決勝前に炸裂した手榴弾

terms.gloss: Vote-stuffing from a single IP address.
terms.why_hard: 2000s forum culture: 'нагнать' is slang for artificially boosting; must read as fraud, not just 'got votes'.

proposed.en: someone pumped in votes from a single IP address
proposed.zh: 有人从同一个IP地址刷票
proposed.ja: 単一のIPアドレスから票を水増しした

terms.gloss: Durov maintained the pose of a neutral referee.
terms.why_hard: The referee framing recurs in Durov's self-presentation as 'ensuring fairness'; should use one consistent role-word.

proposed.en: Durov kept to the role of referee
proposed.zh: 杜罗夫坚守裁判的角色
proposed.ja: ドゥーロフは審判の役割を貫いた

terms.gloss: Claiming not to be on the judging panel.
terms.why_hard: Distinction between jury and arbiter is the whole point of his dodge; both must be distinct terms.

terms.gloss: Bureaucratic doublespeak: 'I merely ensure the fair expression of the people's will' — an election-commission cliché.
terms.why_hard: Sounds like official election rhetoric; keeping the officious tone signals Durov's irony.

proposed.en: merely ensuring the fair expression of the people's will
proposed.zh: 只是保证民意表达的公正性
proposed.ja: 民意の公正な表明を保障するだけ

terms.gloss: Fake/fraudulent votes.
terms.why_hard: Period forum slang; keep a compact coinage used consistently for ballot-stuffing across the book.

terms.gloss: Seven discussion threads sprang up on the student forum.
terms.why_hard: 'Тема' is a forum thread, not 'theme'; and the forum is the earlier-established student forum, needs the same name.

proposed.en: seven threads sprang up on the forum
proposed.zh: 论坛上冒出了七个帖子
proposed.ja: フォーラムにスレッドが七つ立った

terms.gloss: 'The architect' — Durov as designer of the site/contest, whom students suspected of rigging it.
terms.why_hard: Title-epithet for Durov; must match how the book elsewhere calls him creator/architect of the network.

terms.gloss: To draw hatred upon oneself; the students believed Durov engineered the fraud to make himself hated.
terms.why_hard: Inverted PR logic central to Durov's persona — any strong emotion, even hatred, is engagement.

proposed.ja: 自分への憎悪を呼び起こす

terms.gloss: 'What matters is that you stir people' — Durov's credo that any emotional engagement is good.
terms.why_hard: This is a recurring statement of his attention-economy philosophy; one formulation should be reused later in the book.

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the social network Durov founded.
terms.why_hard: Needs a fixed rendering policy (transliterate vs. translate 'in contact') applied book-wide; Chinese/Japanese conventions differ.

terms.gloss: Membership of VKontakte passed ten million.
terms.why_hard: Milestone figure; keep numerals and 'users/members' consistent with network-statistics phrasing used elsewhere.

proposed.en: the count passed the ten-million mark
proposed.ja: 利用者が一千万人を突破した

terms.term: репрессировать группы, разжигающие ненависть к создателю сети
terms.gloss: Ban or punish groups inciting hatred toward the site's creator; 'creator of the network' is Durov's favored self-title.
terms.why_hard: 'Репрессировать' is deliberately Soviet-political vocabulary; 'creator of the network' must match his established epithet.

proposed.en: to repress groups fomenting hatred of the network's creator
proposed.zh: 镇压那些煽动对社交网络创始人仇恨的群组
proposed.ja: ネットワーク創設者への憎悪を煽るグループを弾圧する

terms.gloss: He cancelled the audience-vote (students' choice) category.
terms.why_hard: Must connect back to the 'Miss Audience Sympathies' title; 'nomination' here means contest category, not award nomination.

proposed.ja: 学生投票部門を取りやめた

terms.gloss: Elevated literary cliché (Griboyedov's 'Громокипящий кубок') — the audience seethed and roared.
terms.why_hard: A bookish allusion a Russian reader catches; must choose whether to keep the archaic grandeur or flatten it.

proposed.ja: 観衆は雷鳴のごとく沸き立った

terms.gloss: Ironic use of 'occupied': the front row was taken over by sponsors, the dean and cronies.
terms.why_hard: The military/political verb is deliberate irony; a neutral 'took' loses the mocking tone.

terms.gloss: Vyacheslav Mirilashvili-era associate — here Levon Perekopsky, Durov's close aide.
terms.why_hard: Name transliteration must be stable across the book; also the assistant role should stay implicit as in Russian.

terms.gloss: The dean and the dean's inner circle of hangers-on, court-style epithet.
terms.why_hard: 'Приближенные' evokes a tsar's court; renders the satirical view of university power — keep the courtly flavor.

terms.term: вынос цветов до фонограммы и конферанса кавээнщиков
terms.gloss: Every detail staged, from the flower procession to the recorded soundtrack and KVN comedians' emceeing.
terms.why_hard: KVN (КВН) is Soviet/Russian student comedy league — needs an analogue or brief gloss; 'фонограмма' implies lip-synced playback.

proposed.en: from the flower parade to the backing track and the KVN comedians' patter
proposed.zh: 从献花环节到伴奏音效再到KVN喜剧社的串场
proposed.ja: 花の入場から音源、KVNお笑いチームの司会まで

terms.gloss: They had rehearsed everything in advance.
terms.why_hard: Shows Durov directing the show yet sitting in the audience — the puppet-master motif; keep the theatrical vocabulary.

proposed.ja: すべてを綿密にリハーサルしていた

terms.gloss: Bolshaya Morskaya Street, a major street in central St Petersburg leading toward Palace Square
terms.why_hard: Translators might transliterate inconsistently (Bolshaya Morskaya vs. Big Sea Street) or omit the 'Bolshaya'

proposed.ja: ボルシャヤ・モルスカヤ通り

terms.gloss: Palace Square, the central square of St Petersburg in front of the Winter Palace
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent throughout the book; some might say 'Palace Square' vs 'Dvortsovaya Square'

terms.gloss: Slang for crashing at someone's place, staying over without formal invitation
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render it as 'registered' or 'signed up' from the literal meaning of вписаться

terms.gloss: The wind-tunnel effect created by St Petersburg's arched gateways (подворотни) channeling wind
terms.why_hard: A translator might miss that подворотни are the characteristic arched passageways through St Petersburg apartment blocks, not just 'alleys'

proposed.en: the wind-tunnel throats of the gateways
proposed.zh: 拱门通道如风洞般呼啸
proposed.ja: アーチ門の風の通り道

terms.gloss: Moraines of a glacier — comparing snowdrifts to glacial deposits crawling over the cobblestones
terms.why_hard: The simile is geologically precise; a translator who flattens it to 'like mountains' loses the author's image

terms.gloss: One of the Rostral Columns on Vasilyevsky Island, a St Petersburg landmark with a viewing platform
terms.why_hard: Translators might not know these are specific columns on the Strelka of Vasilyevsky Island, not generic columns; also the idea of sheltering inside/behind one is a local detail

terms.gloss: People wrapped up like 'cases' or 'sheaths' against the cold — a recurring image in this passage (also in [112])
terms.why_hard: The word футляр means a case/sheath; the image is of people bundled so tightly they look like objects in protective cases. Must be consistent with its reuse in [112]

proposed.ja: 鞘に収まったような人々

terms.term: Двери в трамвае стреляли, как красные матросы
terms.gloss: Tram doors slammed like Red sailors — an allusion to the revolutionary sailors of 1917 who fired their weapons
terms.why_hard: The joke layers a sound metaphor (doors banging = shooting) with a historical allusion to Bolshevik sailors; a literal translation loses the humor

proposed.en: The tram doors fired like Red sailors
proposed.zh: 电车门像红色水兵一样开火
proposed.ja: トラムのドアは赤軍水兵のように撃った

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the subject of the biography
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered consistently throughout; some contexts use full name, others surname only

terms.gloss: Copper coins, small change — colloquial word for low-denomination coins
terms.why_hard: Not just 'coins' but specifically cheap copper/small change; connotes triviality

terms.gloss: Occupied (a desk) — used with deliberate military humor for a schoolboy claiming the front row
terms.why_hard: A translator might neutralize it to 'sat at' and lose the ironic register

terms.term: третья строчка снизу яснее не стала
terms.gloss: An aside meaning 'the third line from the bottom hasn't become any clearer' — a self-referential joke about the text itself or about something written on the blackboard
terms.why_hard: This is a meta-textual joke; a translator who treats it as a straightforward statement about a notebook line will miss the humor

proposed.en: the third line from the bottom was no clearer for it
proposed.zh: 倒数第三行依然看不明白
proposed.ja: 下から三行目は相変わらず不明瞭だった

terms.gloss: Scratched/scrawled on the board — нацарапано implies rough, careless writing, not neat writing
terms.why_hard: A translator might use 'written' and lose the connotation of rough, hasty scrawl

terms.gloss: Arched gateways passing through St Petersburg apartment blocks into courtyards, a defining feature of the city's architecture
terms.why_hard: No direct English equivalent; 'archway' or 'gateway' is approximate, and the word recurs in St Petersburg texts

terms.gloss: Tasya, a diminutive of Taisia, a girl who sat next to young Durov in school
terms.why_hard: Diminutive form must be handled consistently; some translators might expand to Taisia or leave as Tasya

terms.gloss: A school satchel/briefcase — the standard Soviet and post-Soviet school bag, a rigid rectangular case
terms.why_hard: Translating as 'briefcase' evokes a business context; 'schoolbag' is more accurate but less specific

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, the book's subject
terms.why_hard: Must be consistently rendered across the whole book; English readers may know him only as 'the Russian Zuckerberg'

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, Durov's close friend and VK co-founder/vice-president
terms.why_hard: Surname is unusual; a careless transliteration might vary (Perekopski/Perekopsky/Perekopskiy)

terms.gloss: VKontakte, Russia's largest social network, founded by Durov in 2006
terms.why_hard: Must decide once whether to use 'VKontakte', 'VK', or a localized equivalent throughout the book

terms.gloss: Cut loose / went wild / lived it up — colloquial for suddenly spending lavishly after being constrained
terms.why_hard: Literal 'tore off' is meaningless; the register is informal and implies a release of pent-up desire for luxury

terms.gloss: A phrase Durov used as a personal mantra/slogan, implying they reshaped the world through VK
terms.why_hard: The ellipsis suggests a longer or repeated phrase; translator must decide whether to render it as a motto or leave it as an incomplete utterance

terms.gloss: Mantra — used figuratively for Durov's repeated ideological credo
terms.why_hard: Not a literal mantra; the word carries a slightly ironic or reverential tone depending on context; must be consistent if it recurs

terms.gloss: Binary code — the idea that human life is being converted into digital data
terms.why_hard: Straightforward term, but part of Durov's philosophical register; should sound grand, not dryly technical

terms.gloss: Wikipedia, cited as an example of self-regulating online communities
terms.why_hard: Minor, but must match whatever form is used elsewhere (Wikipedia vs. the localized name)

terms.gloss: The free internet — Durov's ideological concept of an open, unmonetized information space
terms.why_hard: Recurring concept in the book; must be rendered consistently to track Durov's philosophy

proposed.ja: 自由なインターネット

terms.gloss: Information flows — a key metaphor in Durov's worldview about power and control
terms.why_hard: Recurring metaphor; 'flows' vs 'streams' vs 'currents' must be consistent

terms.gloss: Appanage principalities — medieval Russian feudal fragments; Durov uses it to describe university faculties as isolated fiefdoms
terms.why_hard: Historical allusion to the fragmentation of Kievan Rus; a literal translation may confuse readers unfamiliar with Russian history, but a free translation loses the vividness

terms.gloss: Peterhof, a suburb of St Petersburg where the physics faculty campus of SPbGU is located
terms.why_hard: Readers need to understand this is a remote campus location, not just a random place name; the distance from the city center is the point

terms.gloss: The economics faculty of St Petersburg State University (СПбГУ)
terms.why_hard: Shorthand adjective used as a noun; must be expanded for clarity in translation
