terms.gloss: The law faculty of SPbGU, referred to by its students
terms.why_hard: Same shorthand pattern; must be consistent with how other faculties are named

terms.gloss: History faculty (исторический факультет), common university abbreviation
terms.why_hard: Informal abbreviation; the casual register matters — it's student slang for the faculty

terms.gloss: Petty politicking / political scheming — pejorative term for self-serving political maneuvering
terms.why_hard: Distinct from neutral 'politics'; carries a dismissive, contemptuous tone

terms.gloss: Student council (студенческий совет), a student self-governance body in Russian universities
terms.why_hard: Not identical to Western student unions; it's a formal body with budget authority in the Russian university system

terms.gloss: Trade union committee (профсоюзный комитет) at the faculty level, which controls event budgets
terms.why_hard: A Soviet-era institutional term that persisted in universities; English 'trade union committee' doesn't convey its actual role in student life; must be consistent throughout

terms.gloss: A 'passionary stratum' — allusion to Lev Gumilyov's ethnological theory of пассионарность (passionarity), meaning a driven, energetic minority
terms.why_hard: Deeply culture-specific term from Gumilyov's pseudo-scientific theory; most English readers won't recognize it, but it signals a specific intellectual register

terms.gloss: Student committee (студенческий комитет), another student governance body, distinct from студсовет
terms.why_hard: Must be distinguished from студсовет if both appear; they are different bodies with different functions

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov's student website for course materials
terms.why_hard: Capitalization varies in Russian; must decide whether to keep the domain as-is or localize it

terms.gloss: oral examination/discussion session used in Russian universities
terms.why_hard: No exact English equivalent; 'colloquium' may mislead

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov's father, Valery Durov, a professor of classical philology
terms.why_hard: Not named here; translator must connect this figure to Durov's father consistently

proposed.en: the professor of classical philology (Durov's father)
proposed.zh: 古典语文学教授（杜罗夫之父）
proposed.ja: 古典文献学の教授（ドゥーロフの父）

terms.gloss: nickname for the nook by the philology department named after Professor Durov
terms.why_hard: Possessive/nickname choice must stay consistent across the book

proposed.ja: ドゥーロフ・コーナー

terms.gloss: Russian university sub-department/chair
terms.why_hard: Not 'cathedra'; should be rendered as an academic unit

terms.gloss: conservative faculty who opposed the site
terms.why_hard: 'Conservative' may sound political; here it means academically/technologically conservative

terms.gloss: patchwork compilation, unoriginal cutting and pasting
terms.why_hard: English 'compilation' is too neutral; need pejorative academic-dishonesty sense

terms.gloss: ageism, prejudice against older people
terms.why_hard: Borrowed English word; decide whether to keep as loan or translate native term

terms.gloss: phrase from Durov: old people trapped inside their own mental constructs
terms.why_hard: Must preserve psychological jargon and accusatory tone; avoid literal 'constructs' confusion

proposed.zh: 困在自己观念框架里的人
proposed.ja: 自らの構成概念の内側にいる人々

terms.gloss: dative of 'totem,' a recurring epithet for Durov
terms.why_hard: 'Totem' may strike target readers as odd; must keep or find equivalent idol/image

terms.gloss: English phrase left in Russian; refers to crowdsourcing/web collaboration
terms.why_hard: Decide whether to keep the English, transliterate, or translate into the target language

proposed.ja: マス・コラボレーション

terms.gloss: both fame and a livelihood
terms.why_hard: 'Bread' metaphor may not carry in target; choose idiomatic equivalent

terms.gloss: hydrocarbon company, i.e. oil-and-gas firm
terms.why_hard: Literal 'hydrocarbon office' is too technical/off; need natural corporate register

terms.gloss: Gazprom, Russia's state-controlled gas giant
terms.why_hard: Genitive inflection; need official polished rendering in each target market

proposed.zh: 俄罗斯天然气工业股份公司（Gazprom）

terms.gloss: Bertova, a female acquaintance of Durov; genitive 'Бертовой' appears later
terms.why_hard: Surname gender and transliteration; avoid treating as male or possessive of Bertov

terms.gloss: quoted location nickname 'the School,' likely a St Petersburg university spot
terms.why_hard: Quoted nickname; literal 'school' may lose the local reference

terms.gloss: The experimental school 'Klassy' (Classes) in St Petersburg, a progressive institution with a Renaissance-inspired ethos
terms.why_hard: The word also means 'classrooms' or 'classes' in ordinary Russian, so a translator might lowercase or genericize it and lose the institutional identity

terms.gloss: To build a reputation or life story for oneself; here used in scare quotes suggesting the process was being engineered for them by outsiders
terms.why_hard: The scare quotes signal irony — someone else was constructing their biography, not them; a flat rendering loses the layer of agency

terms.gloss: Professional-technical school (профессионально-техническое училище), a Soviet-era vocational school with low prestige connotations
terms.why_hard: Simply saying 'vocational school' loses the Soviet institutional baggage and the class contrast the author is drawing

terms.gloss: Smolensky Cemetery on Vasilyevsky Island in St Petersburg, one of the city's oldest cemeteries
terms.why_hard: A translator unfamiliar with St Petersburg geography might not realize this is a specific landmark that anchors the school's location

terms.gloss: Dissidents — used metaphorically to describe the school's students and parents as political outsiders resisting authority
terms.why_hard: The word carries heavy Soviet-era political weight; a translator must decide whether to keep the loaded metaphor or soften it

terms.gloss: The Horde — a self-referential or imposed collective name for the school community, evoking a nomadic, unruly mass
terms.why_hard: Capitalized as a proper noun it functions as a group name; a careless translator might render it as a common noun 'horde' and lose the naming function

terms.gloss: Mednikov, likely the director or key figure of the Klassy school
terms.why_hard: A surname appearing without first name; consistency in rendering across the book is essential

terms.gloss: Sanitary-epidemiological station, a Soviet/post-Soviet public health inspection body used here as a tool to shut down the school
terms.why_hard: The term is a single compound in Russian; English needs a phrase, and the translator must convey both the institution and its role as a weapon of pressure

terms.gloss: Chernaya Rechka, a metro station and area in St Petersburg historically famous as the site of Pushkin's fatal duel
terms.why_hard: The name evokes Pushkin's duel for any Russian reader; a translator might simply transliterate without noting the cultural resonance

proposed.ja: チョールナヤ・レーチカ

terms.gloss: Renaissance men — the school's ideology framed its students as modern Renaissance individuals, a deliberate self-mythologization
terms.why_hard: The phrase is part of the school's self-branding; a translator must decide whether to translate literally or find an equivalent that carries the same aspirational weight

terms.gloss: Colloquial/derogatory term for students of a PTU (vocational school), implying low social status
terms.why_hard: The suffix -шники adds dismissive familiarity; a neutral rendering like 'vocational students' loses the contempt embedded in the original

proposed.ja: 職業訓練校の生徒たち

terms.gloss: Broke the locks — a vivid image of forced entry or liberation, depending on perspective
terms.why_hard: The verb 'вскрыла' (opened by force, like a surgeon opening an abscess) is more violent than 'broke'; it implies deliberate, almost surgical action

terms.gloss: Rebellion/revolt — used to describe the school's resistance to closure, elevating a local dispute to the level of uprising
terms.why_hard: The word is historically loaded (Pugachev's rebellion, etc.); choosing 'revolt' vs 'rebellion' vs 'uprising' affects tone across the book

terms.gloss: Rebels/insurgents — the students and teachers who arrived to find the school locked
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent with the rendering of 'бунт'; if 'бунт' is 'revolt' then this should be 'rebels' not 'protesters'

terms.gloss: Servants of the people — an ironic/sarcastic reference to officials (firemen, sanitary inspectors) who enforce closures
terms.why_hard: The phrase is deeply ironic in Russian; a literal translation without tone markers might read as sincere to an English reader

terms.gloss: Griz, likely a nickname or surname of the school's director
terms.why_hard: Unusual name that may be a nickname; must be rendered consistently throughout the book

terms.gloss: No help could be expected from anywhere — a fixed expression expressing total isolation
terms.why_hard: The construction 'неоткуда' (there is no source from which) is more absolute than 'they couldn't expect help'; it implies structural hopelessness

proposed.en: there was no one to turn to for help
proposed.ja: 助けを期待するすべもなかった

terms.gloss: To tame — used of authorities attempting to domesticate the wild, independent school
terms.why_hard: The metaphor of taming an animal is deliberate; it connects to the 'Horde' metaphor and the overall framing of the school as untamed

terms.gloss: Firemen — colloquial form (standard would be 'пожарные'); here part of a list of officials who burst into classes
terms.why_hard: The colloquial register signals informality and perhaps the children's perspective; a formal translation loses that layer

terms.gloss: On an October morning — possibly echoing revolutionary imagery (October Revolution) given the context of rebellion and lockout
terms.why_hard: The capitalization and placement may evoke the October Revolution; a translator must decide whether to preserve the echo or treat it as simple chronology

terms.gloss: The 'Strange People'—an epithet for Durov's programming team, likely a recurring chapter motif.
terms.why_hard: Capitalized in Russian suggests a proper nickname, not just a description; translating as merely 'strange people' loses the collective identity.

terms.gloss: A tight-knit group or clique, slightly derogatory or ironic, often implying exclusivity.
terms.why_hard: Must not be confused with 'код' (code); it is a slang term for a gang or clique, not a technical term.

terms.gloss: Nerds, geeks, or bookish students (from 'botany' students, implying studiousness).
terms.why_hard: Register is schoolyard slang; should not be rendered as formal 'botanists' or overly harsh 'dorks'.

terms.gloss: Paul Graham, programmer and essayist, influential in tech startup culture.
terms.why_hard: Transliteration varies; must recognize the reference to the specific essay 'Why Nerds Are Unpopular'.

terms.gloss: Title of a famous 2003 essay by Paul Graham on hacker culture and school hierarchy.
terms.why_hard: Should remain in English or be translated according to the target language's convention for foreign essays.

proposed.ja: 『Why Nerds Are Unpopular（オタクがモテない理由）』

terms.gloss: Physics Olympiad (competitive academic contests for school students).
terms.why_hard: Implies a specific culture of competitive academic excellence in Russia, not just a generic science fair.

terms.gloss: Founded their own state (metaphor for an autonomous, isolated community).
terms.why_hard: Hyperbolic metaphor for the team's insularity; literal translation might confuse readers expecting geopolitical content.

proposed.ja: 独自の国家を樹立した

terms.gloss: Nerds (loanword from English, used ironically/affectionately for the programmers).
terms.why_hard: Distinct from 'ботаники'; direct English loanword with slightly different connotation (tech-focused).

terms.gloss: Orange juice vending machine (automatic juicer).
terms.why_hard: Specific period detail of office/startup culture; 'автомат' alone could be misread as 'automatic' (weapon) or 'slot machine'.

proposed.ja: オレンジジュースの自動販売機

terms.gloss: C++ programming language.
terms.why_hard: Standard notation; should not be translated or altered.

terms.gloss: Lead programmer or chief developer.
terms.why_hard: Title within the team hierarchy; should be consistent with other segments referring to technical roles.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the subject of the biography.

terms.gloss: The younger Durov brother (Nikolai), fluent talker, not claiming the tech lead
terms.why_hard: If rendered as a name-free 'junior' it collides with job titles later

terms.gloss: Café Rubai on Nevsky, named after Omar Khayyam's rubaiyat
terms.why_hard: Keep the Persian literary name; don't translate as 'quatrains café'

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the social network (later VK)
terms.why_hard: Book-wide choice: VKontakte vs VK vs In Contact; quotes and gender of site

terms.gloss: Nevsky Prospect, Petersburg's main avenue of cafés

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte and the central subject of the biography.
terms.why_hard: Inflected forms of his surname must all use the same established rendering.

terms.gloss: Yuri Milner, the technology investor behind Digital Sky Technologies.

terms.gloss: Literally “sweet-cherry juice,” the chapter title and likely a motif developed in the chapter.

proposed.ja: 百五十平方メートル近くもある

terms.gloss: A colloquial abbreviation for социальная сеть, meaning a social-networking service.
terms.why_hard: It refers to the online service rather than an abstract network of social relations, and its casual register should be retained.

terms.gloss: Overly abstract, fine-grained theorizing about product and technical principles.

proposed.ja: スコラ哲学めいた議論

terms.gloss: Lev Leviev, an early VKontakte investor and shareholder arriving at the apartment.
terms.why_hard: The given name alone does not identify him for an outsider and can also be mistaken for the Russian noun meaning “lion.”

terms.gloss: A covered passage driven through the street-facing part of a building into its inner courtyard.
terms.why_hard: It is a characteristic urban architectural feature, not simply an alley, gateway, or front door.

proposed.en: the covered passageway into the courtyard
proposed.ja: 中庭へ抜ける建物下の通路

terms.gloss: The offices and residential apartments associated with the banker Blokk, a former occupant and renovator of the building.
terms.why_hard: Контора is a period business office, while Blokk's identity and the building's history require external verification.

proposed.en: the offices and apartments of the banker Blokk
proposed.zh: 银行家布洛克的事务所和住宅
proposed.ja: 銀行家ブロックの事務所と住居

terms.gloss: Architectural personifications on the façade representing Justice and the legal profession or bar.

proposed.en: allegorical figures of Justice and the Bar

terms.gloss: A shareholder in Durov's company, here referring to Lev Leviev's formal stake in VKontakte.

terms.gloss: Mikhail Bunin, the programmer-blogger ('mensrea') consulted by the Durov brothers in VKontakte's early days
terms.why_hard: A translator might confuse him with the writer Ivan Bunin; he recurs as a source throughout the book and needs one fixed name form

terms.gloss: Recurring in-book epithet for Bunin (a 'minstrel' of the IT scene, echoing his blog persona and 'Bardin's minstrels' culture)
terms.why_hard: A literal 'minstrel' reads as nonsense in English; dropping it loses a running motif that must stay consistent book-wide

terms.gloss: Nikolai Durov, Pavel's older brother, VKontakte's chief technical architect
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered consistently with 'Дуров-старший' and 'Дуровы' elsewhere; the kinship structure matters

terms.gloss: 'Durov the elder' — Nikolai, the older brother, echoing Russian patronymic-style press usage
terms.why_hard: A careless rendering might make him Pavel's father; the -старший/-младший pair must be tracked across the book

terms.gloss: The Durov brothers (Pavel and Nikolai) as a pair
terms.why_hard: Plural family name in Russian could be misread as the whole family rather than the two brothers

terms.gloss: Apache HTTP Server, the classic open-source web server
terms.why_hard: Should stay as the brand name Apache, not 'Apache server' translated

terms.gloss: Nginx, the high-load web server created by Igor Sysoev, later the load-balancing backbone of VKontakte
terms.why_hard: Latin spelling varies (nginx/NGINX/Nginx); pick one form and keep it

terms.gloss: VKontakte, Russia's largest social network, founded by Pavel Durov in 2006
terms.why_hard: Book-wide choice between VKontakte, VK, and localized forms must be uniform

terms.gloss: HighLoad++, an annual Russian conference on high-traffic web engineering, held 2011 in Moscow
terms.why_hard: An invented-looking name; readers won't know it's a real conference series and the name shouldn't be translated

terms.gloss: Andrei Illarionov, a VKontakte developer who presented its load-distribution system at HighLoad-2011
terms.why_hard: Not the famous Putin adviser of the same name; a low-profile engineer needing correct fixed rendering

proposed.ja: アンドレイ・イラリオノフ

terms.gloss: 2000s internet slang: to get up to speed on a subject, absorb it fast
terms.why_hard: Colloquial register; a formal rendering kills the narrator's ironic voice

terms.gloss: Simile: winning programming olympiads is like learning bayonet thrusts on a dummy — drill, not real combat
terms.why_hard: The whole point (school exercises vs real-world scaling war) must survive; a translator might keep the image but lose the 'training dummy' sense

proposed.en: like learning to bayonet a dummy
proposed.ja: 藁人形に銃剣を突く訓練のようなもの

terms.gloss: 'The Taming of Traffic' — pun on the Russian title of The Taming of the Shrew (Укрощение строптивой)
terms.why_hard: English loses the Shakespeare allusion unless rephrased; the battle/bataille framing continues the military metaphor chain

proposed.en: Taming traffic that grows geometrically is a different battle
proposed.zh: 驯服几何级增长的流量是另一场战役
proposed.ja: 急増するトラフィックを手なずけるのは、別の戦いなのだ

terms.gloss: Archaic Russian word for 'battle', ironic-elevated register
terms.why_hard: Part of the mock-epic military register (азов, баталия) that should be kept consistently elevated-ironic

terms.gloss: The ABCs, the basics (from 'alpha and omega' / Cyrillic az)
terms.why_hard: Fixed idiom; must match how the book renders other 'beginner' references

terms.gloss: Diminutive 'little message' — ironic folksy tone for Nikolai's short message

terms.gloss: 'Half a week' — colloquial way to say several days
terms.why_hard: Must preserve the casual imprecision, not turn into an exact '3.5 days'

terms.gloss: Engineer slang: fine-tuned the settings
terms.why_hard: Colloquial technical register; literal 'twisted the screws/parameters' is wrong

proposed.ja: パラメータを調整した

proposed.en: We showed them where to dig — and they dug us under.

terms.gloss: Packed-to-the-rafters hall
terms.why_hard: Vivid colloquial idiom; literal 'stuffed full' reads oddly

terms.gloss: Load-balancing/distribution system, VKontakte's much-admired infrastructure

terms.gloss: Roman Simonov, a partner at Delta Private Equity Partners, a Russian PE fund active in the mid-2000s

terms.gloss: A Russian private equity firm that invested in tech and media companies in the 2000s
terms.why_hard: Must be kept as a proper name in Latin script; a translator might attempt to translate 'Delta' or 'Private Equity'

proposed.ja: デルタ・プライベート・エクイティ・パートナーズ

terms.gloss: Albert Popkov, founder of Odnoklassniki.ru, the social network that preceded VKontakte in Russia

proposed.ja: アルベルト・ポプコフ

terms.gloss: Odnoklassniki (Classmates), a Russian social networking site founded in 2006, a direct competitor to VKontakte
terms.why_hard: The name literally means 'classmates'; a translator must decide whether to transliterate or translate, and stay consistent throughout the book

terms.gloss: A Latvian company that was an early investor in Odnoklassniki
terms.why_hard: The text calls the partners 'Latvians from Forticom'; a translator needs to know Forticom was a Latvian IT firm to render the context correctly

terms.gloss: Vyacheslav (Slava) Mirilashvili and Lev Leviev, the two co-founders/investors of VKontakte alongside Durov
terms.why_hard: These are diminutives; a translator must decide whether to use full names or keep the informal forms, and must be consistent with how they appear elsewhere

terms.gloss: Yuri Milner, Russian-Israeli venture capitalist, founder of DST Global, early investor in Facebook, Twitter, Groupon
terms.why_hard: Well-known figure but a careless translator might misspell or confuse with other Milners; his role as 'venture capitalist' is stated explicitly here

terms.gloss: Mail.ru Group (later VK), the Russian internet conglomerate that Milner led; it acquired Odnoklassniki and Astrum
terms.why_hard: Must remain in Latin script; a translator might be tempted to render it as 'Mail.ru Group' or add context not in the original

terms.gloss: Astrum Online Entertainment, a Russian online gaming holding company acquired by Mail.ru
terms.why_hard: A translator might not know Astrum was specifically a gaming holding and might leave it unexplained or add incorrect context

terms.gloss: Venture capitalist; the text uses this as a descriptor for Milner
terms.why_hard: The Russian calque 'венчурный капиталист' is slightly awkward; a translator should use the natural English term 'venture capitalist' rather than a literal back-translation

proposed.ja: ベンチャーキャピタリスト

terms.gloss: 'Under the banners of' — a military/imperial metaphor meaning to gather or consolidate under one's control

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, subject of the biography, here called by surname only
terms.why_hard: the surname transliteration must be fixed once (Durov) for the whole book

terms.gloss: Steve Jobs, in a comparison planted in the reader's mind
terms.why_hard: must be recognised as Steve Jobs and given the standard exonym in each language

terms.gloss: the 1999 TNT docudrama about Jobs and Gates, whose opening scene features a director being steered by Jobs
terms.why_hard: a careless translator may assume the Disney pirate franchise rather than the 1999 TV film

proposed.ja: 「パイレーツ・オブ・シリコンバレー」

terms.why_hard: каналы reads as gutter-like plumbing unless rendered as communications channels

terms.gloss: 'homunculus identities' — the millions of little artificial selves created online
terms.why_hard: homunculus must be understood as the alchemical artificial man, not a gnome or bot

proposed.ja: ホムンクルス式のアイデンティティ

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the social network at the centre of the book
terms.why_hard: settle once between Anglicised 'VKontakte', Cyrillic script, and the later abbreviation VK

terms.term: so long, and thanks for all the fish
terms.gloss: dolphins' farewell line quoted in English in the source; also the title of Adams's fourth novel
terms.why_hard: the stray English sentence is a fixed literary allusion, not an author's joke to be retranslated loosely

proposed.en: so long, and thanks for all the fish
proposed.ja: さようなら、そして魚をありがとう

terms.gloss: the Russian release title of Adams's fourth Hitchhiker novel, given in the footnote
terms.why_hard: each target language must use its official published book title, not a literal rendering

proposed.en: So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish
proposed.ja: 『さようなら、そして魚をありがとう』

terms.gloss: Douglas Adams, named in the footnote
terms.why_hard: plain, but his standard exonym must be kept consistent across the three languages

terms.gloss: the series title conventionally rendered 'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy'
terms.why_hard: a literal 'hitchhiking through the galaxy' would ignore the canonical published title

proposed.en: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
proposed.ja: 『銀河ヒッチハイク・ガイド』

terms.gloss: the Vogons, the demolition-bureaucrat aliens in Adams's series
terms.why_hard: the alien race name needs its canonical target-language form, not a phonetic guess

terms.gloss: Adams's 'hyperspatial express route', part of the same allusion
terms.why_hard: back-translating literally risks missing the canonical wording of the original English joke

terms.gloss: chapter title naming the Botanical Garden, i.e. its St Petersburg neighbourhood
terms.why_hard: must be handled as a proper local name or a generic garden, once, and localisation for context-free readers decided

terms.gloss: Cervantes — the boy carries a volume of Cervantes
terms.why_hard: clarify it is the author in the genitive, not a work; use the fixed exonym

terms.gloss: the entrance/stairwell of an apartment block, a fixture of Russian housing
terms.why_hard: English 'porch' or 'doorway' misplaces it; needs a natural housing term once

terms.gloss: colloquial Russian 'face' (wind blowing in his mug)
terms.why_hard: a literal 'physiognomy' is nonsense; the ja register decision matters

terms.gloss: St Petersburg, affectionately shortened the way locals say it
terms.why_hard: decide once between full 'St Petersburg' and the colloquial short form for each language

terms.gloss: the author's running way of referring to Durov as 'the hero/protagonist'
terms.why_hard: English 'hero' can read as moral praise; one gloss must be fixed for the recurrence

terms.gloss: 'a potent salesman of ideas' — Durov's characteristic persuasive pitchmanship
terms.why_hard: literal 'strong-acting salesman' is awkward; the characterising phrasing should be settled once

proposed.zh: 一位极具说服力的“点子推销员”
proposed.ja: きわめて強力な「アイデアのセールスマン」

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, VKontakte founder, and his brother Nikolai Durov, co-founder and technical architect
terms.why_hard: Both brothers recur throughout the book; surname inflection ('the Durovs') and who does what must stay consistent

proposed.zh: 帕维尔和尼古拉·杜罗夫兄弟
proposed.ja: パーヴェルとニコライ・ドゥーロフ兄弟

terms.gloss: VKontakte.ru, the social network the Durovs launched in 2006 (later vk.com)
terms.why_hard: The segment uses both the .ru spelling and the leading underscore from a quoted post; a translator must decide how to render early-2000s URLs and whether to transliterate or keep Latin

terms.gloss: 'My Faculty', a short-lived St Petersburg student social network and VKontakte's first direct competitor
terms.why_hard: The author alternates between the URL and 'our site' (the blogger's own); the possessive framing must be preserved because it signals who is speaking

terms.gloss: hacker attack; here the 2006 accusation that Durov's team hacked the rival site
terms.why_hard: The word 'криминальная хакерская атака' is deliberately inflated blogger rhetoric; translating flatly loses the accusatory hyperbole of the original post

terms.gloss: 'criminal' — the rival blogger's loaded framing of the alleged hack as a crime
terms.why_hard: In 2006 Russian internet speech this was rhetorical escalation, not a legal claim; keeping the slightly absurd solemnity matters for tone

terms.gloss: to hack/break into a site; the site 'was hacked and stopped working'
terms.why_hard: Standard term but recurs constantly in the VK-wars chapters; en 'hack' vs 'crack', zh 入侵 vs 破解 must be fixed once for the whole book

terms.gloss: security vulnerability in a website
terms.why_hard: Technical security jargon that must match the register of a bug-bounty style request; 'проверить на уязвимость' = test for vulnerabilities

proposed.zh: 检测两个网站的安全漏洞

terms.gloss: informal hacker slang for security holes / exploitable flaws
terms.why_hard: Colloquial register inside a quoted post; a formal rendering like 'vulnerabilities' flattens the voice of the quote

terms.gloss: henchman / underling — the rival's dismissive word for whoever posted on Durov's behalf
terms.why_hard: Pejorative 'sidekick/footman' connotation; neutral 'assistant' would miss the sneer

terms.gloss: tall tales, anecdotes one spreads; here myths that 'they hacked us'
terms.why_hard: Colloquial diminutive of 'tale'; 'stories' is too neutral, 'lies' too strong; ja rendering must catch the wry register

terms.gloss: Yandex.Blogs, Yandex's blog search aggregator service, cited as documentary 'evidence'
terms.why_hard: Defunct service; en/zh/ja readers won't know it aggregated blog posts rather than hosting them — that is what made it 'searchable proof'

proposed.ja: ヤンデックス・ブログ検索

terms.gloss: blog author handle posting the accusation, dated 4.12.2006
terms.why_hard: A pseudonymous forum nickname; must be kept verbatim, not localized, since other segments quote the same handle

terms.gloss: 'I sent the hackers packing' — i.e. refused/rebuffed them, Russian euphemistic idiom
terms.why_hard: 'Послать' here means 'told them to get lost', not 'dispatched'; a literal rendering reverses the meaning entirely

proposed.en: I told them to get lost

terms.gloss: 'the hapless/unlucky competitor' — mocking epithet for MoiFakultet's owner
terms.why_hard: Irony-laden epithet; 'hapless rival' is the recurring mocking tone toward failed VK competitors and must stay consistent

terms.gloss: the recurring 2006–07 accusation that VKontakte copied its design/features from rivals
terms.why_hard: A standing charge in the VK founding myth; the paragraph header style ('КРИМИНАЛ.' / 'ПЛАГИАТ.') mimics a press-release structure and should be kept

terms.gloss: 2000s Runet colloquialism for email addresses / user emails
terms.why_hard: Anglicism written in Cyrillic; signals the era's slangy net-speak, best rendered as 'email addresses' but with awareness it is colloquial

terms.gloss: 'I'll pay' — terse bounty offer in the quoted hack-for-hire post
terms.why_hard: The clipped 'the $ is on me' is period forum idiom; a translator must keep it sounding like a forum post, not a contract

proposed.en: there's money in it for you from me

terms.gloss: site audience/user base — the metric startups competed over in 2006
terms.why_hard: Recurring startup-industry term; 'audience' vs 'user base' choice must be fixed for the whole book

terms.gloss: 'magnanimous' — Durov implying he was generous in not retaliating
terms.why_hard: Slightly archaic, self-flattering word choice typical of Durov's public voice; keep the lofty tone

terms.term: [сейчас ничего криминального по этой ссылке найти невозможно. – Н. К.]

terms.gloss: quest (video game slang used by Durov for ambitious real-world ventures)
terms.why_hard: Gamer parlance applied to entrepreneurial ventures (foreshadowing Telegram)

terms.gloss: Durov ruthlessly purged dissent within his team
terms.why_hard: figurative scorched-earth idiom, must not be translated literally

proposed.ja: デュロフは容赦なく排除した

terms.gloss: old-timer, veteran team member

terms.gloss: the intense pace/culture of startup work

proposed.ja: スタートアップのペース

terms.gloss: recurring epithet for Durov as team's totem/idol figure
terms.why_hard: recurring epithet across book, must render consistently as capitalized title

terms.gloss: a designer/architect's chair, likely a specific stylish office chair type
terms.why_hard: specific furniture connotation of trendy/expensive office aesthetic

terms.gloss: grabbed by the collar/lapels aggressively

terms.gloss: submitted resignation letter
terms.why_hard: standard phrase but should stay consistent as formal resignation language

terms.gloss: anniversary of VKontakte's founding
terms.why_hard: must clarify which anniversary/network without over-explaining

terms.gloss: Durov's birthday, coinciding with VK's anniversary
terms.why_hard: factual detail; must remain consistent with known Durov birthdate

terms.gloss: table overflowing/laden with fruit

terms.gloss: no alcohol or cigarettes at the party, reflecting Durov's abstemious/health-conscious rules
terms.why_hard: signals corporate culture/personal ideology, should not read as random detail

proposed.en: there was no alcohol or cigarettes
proposed.ja: 酒もタバコもなかった

terms.gloss: flipped the middle finger at the camera / made an obscene gesture
terms.why_hard: English loanword 'fuck' used as gesture description in Russian text; must decide whether to keep English word or describe gesture

proposed.zh: 对着镜头做了个粗鲁手势（竖中指）
proposed.ja: カメラに向かって中指を立てた

terms.gloss: recurring epithet for the VK team/programmers, likely referencing 'Valkyrie' internal codename or gaming culture
terms.why_hard: obscure in-house reference; needs research into VK team lore to translate faithfully

proposed.ja: ワルキューレの仲間たち

terms.gloss: the communication tool, i.e. VKontakte itself
terms.why_hard: understated euphemism for the platform, should stay consistent with other references to VK as 'the tool'

proposed.ja: そのコミュニケーションツール

terms.gloss: representatives of the state/government
terms.why_hard: vague but politically loaded phrase referencing Durov's dealings with Russian authorities

terms.gloss: toiled day and night
terms.why_hard: standard idiom for relentless work, should be rendered naturally not stiffly

proposed.ja: 昼夜を問わず取り組んでいた

terms.gloss: became furious/enraged
terms.why_hard: intensity word establishing Durov's temper motif, consistency with his other rage scenes

terms.gloss: chewing on sausage—casual, unpretentious eating detail
terms.why_hard: small realist detail signaling informality; risk of over-translating as odd

proposed.en: chewing on a piece of sausage
proposed.ja: ソーセージを噛みながら

terms.gloss: piece of melon Durov was eating when photographed
terms.why_hard: minor visual detail, should stay consistent with fruit-table motif

terms.gloss: the guys invited their girlfriends to the party
terms.why_hard: reflects gendered office culture detail, should be phrased naturally not awkwardly literal

proposed.ja: 男たちは彼女を連れてきた

terms.gloss: the programmers/engineers of VK team
terms.why_hard: recurring group term, consistency with 'друзья валькирий' and team epithets

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte and the speaker answering the interviewer here.
terms.why_hard: His surname should follow the project-wide form and not be translated or reordered inconsistently.

terms.gloss: Allied with or dependent on the same powerful business partners, with shared interests and risks.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering can obscure the implication that Durov is tied to these people despite differing values.

terms.gloss: Their methods belong to Russia's violent, lawless 1990s era of oligarchic and criminalized capitalism.
terms.why_hard: Merely saying “their style is from the nineties” misses the specifically post-Soviet associations of coercion, racketeering, and ruthless dealmaking.

proposed.en: Their methods are straight out of Russia’s wild nineties
proposed.zh: 他们还是俄罗斯“狂野九十年代”那套作风
proposed.ja: 彼らのやり方は、ロシアの「荒れた九〇年代」そのものです

terms.gloss: The large-scale redistribution and seizure of assets during post-Soviet privatization and subsequent corporate conflicts.
terms.why_hard: A neutral phrase such as “property reallocation” loses the connotations of oligarchic takeovers, coercion, and disputed ownership.

proposed.en: the vast post-Soviet carve-ups of property
proposed.zh: 后苏联时代大规模的资产瓜分
proposed.ja: ソ連崩壊後の大規模な資産再分配

terms.gloss: They have privileged access to senior officials and the political power centered in the Kremlin.
terms.why_hard: The “reception rooms” are metonymic; translating them literally would understate elite political access and connections.

proposed.en: have access to the corridors of Kremlin power
proposed.zh: 能出入克里姆林宫的权力圈
proposed.ja: クレムリン中枢に出入りできる

terms.gloss: To cultivate emotional detachment from the outcome so that fear of losing the company cannot be used as leverage.
terms.why_hard: “Отрешенность” can sound religious or apathetic, whereas here it means deliberate nonattachment in negotiation.

proposed.zh: 让自己做到超然、不执着于结果
proposed.ja: 結果に執着しない境地に達する

terms.term: Вы же помните, в какой стране живете
terms.gloss: A veiled threat that in Russia powerful people can bypass formal law and inflict consequences.
terms.why_hard: As a literal reminder of location it sounds innocuous; Russian readers hear cynical intimidation about arbitrary power and weak legal protections.

proposed.en: You do remember what country you’re living in, don’t you?
proposed.zh: 你可别忘了自己是在什么国家
proposed.ja: 自分がどんな国に住んでいるか、忘れてはいないでしょうね

terms.gloss: To ruin his reputation decisively and leave no prospect of restoring it.
terms.why_hard: The Russian “put a cross on” idiom should not be rendered as a literal religious act.

terms.gloss: Durov says he will not submit, yield under pressure, or compromise his principles.
terms.why_hard: The physical image of bending carries a defiant colloquial force that can become either too literal or too mild.

proposed.ja: それでも私は屈しない

terms.gloss: Barack Obama, then U.S. president seeking re-election in 2012
terms.why_hard: Name is obvious but the book’s Russian inflections and the 2012 campaign frame must stay consistent with earlier Obama mentions

terms.gloss: raising money for a political campaign (calque of English fundraising)
terms.why_hard: фондирование is a 2010s Russian anglicism; ‘funding’ vs ‘fundraising’ vs ‘financing’ changes the campaign sense

terms.gloss: admits he doesn’t get / isn’t fluent in mobile (phones and apps)
terms.why_hard: рубить is youth slang for ‘to grasp’; мобайл in quotes is English ‘mobile’ as a domain, not a device brand

terms.gloss: political technologist / campaign strategist (Russian term for consultants who run elections as operations)
terms.why_hard: политтехнолог is post-Soviet jargon, not identical to U.S. ‘campaign manager’ or ‘political consultant’

terms.gloss: Jim Messina, Obama 2012 campaign manager
terms.why_hard: Cyrillic Мессина can be misspelled Messina/Messina; role must match later mentions

terms.gloss: Larry Page, Google co-founder
terms.why_hard: Пейдж vs Page; genitive Пейджу must not become a different romanization mid-book

terms.gloss: internet-era tech sages / Silicon Valley gurus consulted for campaign strategy
terms.why_hard: гуру is both ironic and honorific in 2010s Russian tech prose; ‘guru’ vs ‘expert’ vs ‘thought leader’

proposed.ja: インターネットのカリスマ

terms.gloss: multi-level marketing; pyramid-style recruit-ten-who-recruit-ten structure
terms.why_hard: Latin MLM is left untranslated in Russian; readers need the pyramid/network-marketing analogue, not a footnote

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte
terms.why_hard: Must stay the same surname form as elsewhere; never ‘Duroff’ or given-name-only

terms.gloss: the large shiny globe in VK’s St Petersburg office, a recurring spatial marker
terms.why_hard: Literal ‘globe’ without office context looks like Earth or a toy; it is a landmark in this book

terms.gloss: kept pushing his fear farther away from (the globe / the office)
terms.why_hard: гнать страх is not ‘drive out fear’ in the usual sense; it is spatial, almost comic

proposed.en: kept driving the fear farther from
proposed.zh: 把恐惧继续往地球仪外赶
proposed.ja: 恐怖を地球儀からさらに遠ざけた

terms.gloss: Alexei Navalny, opposition lawyer and anti-corruption activist
terms.why_hard: Name spelling (Navalny vs Navalnyi) and whether to gloss his role must be book-wide

proposed.ja: アレクセイ・ナワリヌイ

terms.gloss: his public identity then: lawyer and anti-corruption campaigner
terms.why_hard: Hyphenated Russian epithet; over-translating as ‘crusader’ or under-translating as just ‘lawyer’

terms.gloss: RosPil, Navalny’s 2010s crowdsourced anti-graft project (pun on raspil, embezzlement)
terms.why_hard: Transliterate vs translate the pun; readers need the same form every time it appears

terms.gloss: Good Propaganda Machine, Navalny’s viral political-media project
terms.why_hard: Title must be fixed; ‘kind/good’ vs ‘nice’ and whether to keep Russian in quotes

proposed.ja: 「善良なプロパガンダ・マシン」

terms.gloss: VK group membership cap that Navalny’s support group had hit
terms.why_hard: Not a legal ‘limit’ on speech; a product quota Durov ordered lifted

terms.gloss: Lenta.ru, then a major independent Russian news site that ran Durov’s column
terms.why_hard: Keep site name stable (Lenta.ru vs Lenta); it is not ‘the ribbon’

terms.gloss: users, in 2000s RuNet geek register (not нейтральные пользователи)
terms.why_hard: Dropping to ‘users’ loses voice; calquing ‘uzers’ is unreadable in EN/ZH/JA

terms.gloss: Facebook, the rival network Durov feared would absorb VK groups
terms.why_hard: Later Meta/Facebook split; this book’s 2013 world is still ‘Facebook’

terms.gloss: Mail.ru Group, the holding then tightening control over VK
terms.why_hard: Must match earlier renderings (Mail.ru vs Mail.ru Group vs VK’s owner)

terms.gloss: not quite a materialist: he claims a mystical, not purely causal, view of his own motives
terms.why_hard: ‘Materialist’ in philosophy vs ‘materialistic’ (greedy); easy false friend

proposed.ja: 完全な唯物論者ではない

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, the book's subject.
terms.why_hard: Name transliteration varies (Durov/Durow); must match the rest of the book.

terms.gloss: VKontakte, Russia's largest social network, founded by Durov.
terms.why_hard: Whether to use the brand 'VK', the transliteration 'VKontakte', or a gloss like 'In Touch' must be fixed once for the whole book.

terms.gloss: A nickname ('Totem') used in the book for a business partner/figure who was financing data centers; a recurring epithet.
terms.why_hard: It is a nickname, not a real name; a careless translator renders it as the word 'totem' without marking it as this person's standing epithet.

terms.gloss: A figure on the opposing side in the servers dispute (the one Durov accuses); in the book's context, involved in the 2011 conflict around VK's servers.
terms.why_hard: Common Russian surname; must be identified and romanized consistently, and the reader must grasp he is the adversary, not a neutral party.

terms.gloss: Tennis metaphor: a 'lob' (свеча) put up over the court, which Durov happily 'extinguished' — i.e. he spiked the opponent's counter-accusation.
terms.why_hard: Untranslatable pun ( свеча = candle / tennis lob; гасить = put out a candle); literal translation is nonsense, and 'корт' here doubles as tennis court.

proposed.en: happily smashed down the lob his opponent had sent over the court
proposed.zh: 轻松扣杀了对方抛起的high吊球（把对方的反击当场拍死）
proposed.ja: 相手が打ち上げたロブを笑って叩き落とした

terms.gloss: 'Slick/slippery manager' — Durov's recurring dismissive label for evasive corporate types.
terms.why_hard: 'Скользкий' is a recurring epithet in the book and must stay consistently slimy-slippery, not become 'cunning' or 'shifty'.

terms.gloss: Dividing the world by values into 'ours' and 'theirs' — an us-vs-them worldview; Durov does this with people and companies.
terms.why_hard: The 'свои/чужие' opposition is a deep Russian cultural frame (also folklore: 'свой–чужой') that must read as worldview, not mere friendship.

terms.gloss: Durov's idol framed as a military commander — Jobs as a general whose campaigns he admires.
terms.why_hard: The military register colors the whole quote that follows; dropping it flattens the mock-warlike tone of Durov's speech.

proposed.ja: 将軍とも言うべき憧れの人

terms.gloss: A Soviet 'sixtier' — the idealistic liberal generation of the 1960s Thaw; Durov retroactively enrols Steve Jobs in it.
terms.why_hard: Pure Soviet-cultural label applied to an American; the whole point is Durov's Soviet-lens view of Jobs, which needs a gloss or analogue, not deletion.

proposed.en: a sixtier, one of the Soviet-style idealists of the sixties
proposed.zh: 六十年代理想主义者（苏联‘六十年代人’）

terms.gloss: Apple's famous '1984' Super Bowl ad (Ridley Scott), casting IBM as Orwell's Big Brother.
terms.why_hard: Reader must connect it to the very next clause about fighting IBM; translating just as 'the 1984 ad' without the Orwell/Apple frame loses the rebellion theme of the whole passage.

terms.gloss: Apple's self-image as pirates (the original pirate flag over the Mac team's building), rebels against the establishment.
terms.why_hard: The pirate metaphor runs through the book's portrait of VK as rebels; must keep the flag lore implicit, not turn into 'hacker'.

proposed.ja: アップルは海賊だった

terms.gloss: IBM, transliterated into Russian slang and called 'rotten' — Apple's old enemy cast as decayed.
terms.why_hard: Both the russified transliteration and the 'rotten' register matter: Durov speaks of IBM as something gone off, an epithet repeated in 'тухлый дизайн' below.

terms.gloss: Parody of Soviet bureaucratic phraseology: a product 'capturing broad strata of the population', i.e. mass-market takeover told in party-speak.
terms.why_hard: The joke is the register — Soviet propaganda clichés describing Apple marketing; a straight business rendering ('mass adoption') kills the irony.

proposed.en: The product's conquest of the broad masses of the population
proposed.zh: 产品对广大人民群众的占领
proposed.ja: 製品による広範な人民層の制圧

terms.gloss: Durov's recurring enemy-list: 'rotten design' and 'wholesale monetisation', the same decay vocabulary as his IBM jibe.
terms.why_hard: The decay metaphors (тухлый/протухший) must be consistent with the IBM epithet above, and 'повальная' (an epidemic of monetisation) should keep the plague register.

proposed.en: putrid design and the monetisation craze
proposed.zh: 腐臭的设计与泛滥的变现
proposed.ja: 腐ったデザインと全面化したマネタイズ

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, the book's subject
terms.why_hard: Must stay the same surname form as the rest of the book, never 'Duroff' or given-name-only

terms.gloss: Durov's apartment on Sennaya (Haymarket) Square, central St Petersburg
terms.why_hard: Сенная is a toponym, not 'hay square' calqued; must match other Sennaya mentions

terms.gloss: Sennaya Square / Haymarket district in St Petersburg
terms.why_hard: Transliteration vs translation (Haymarket) would split the map for readers

terms.gloss: the downside/worst-case path of events, startup-speak of the era
terms.why_hard: Calquing 'negative scenario' sounds like film; it is risk-talk, not cinema

proposed.ja: ネガティブ・シナリオ

terms.term: ты на самом деле ничем не владеешь
terms.gloss: you don't really own anything (stoic/memento-mori ownership line)
terms.why_hard: владеешь is legal-own, not 'have'; flattening it loses the property-rights sting

proposed.zh: 你其实什么都不真正拥有
proposed.ja: 実際には何も所有していない

terms.term: потерять то, что у тебя якобы есть
terms.gloss: be ready to lose what you only supposedly possess
terms.why_hard: якобы marks illusory possession; 'supposedly' vs 'allegedly' changes tone

proposed.en: lose what you only supposedly have
proposed.zh: 失去你自以为拥有的东西
proposed.ja: あると思い込んでいるものを失う

terms.term: ветхие мехи прохудятся и вино выльется само
terms.gloss: allusion to new wine bursting old wineskins (Gospels); old vessels fail and the wine spills of itself
terms.why_hard: Must stay recognizably biblical, not a random leaky-bag image; 'wineskins' not 'fur'

proposed.en: the old wineskins will split and the wine will spill of itself
proposed.zh: 旧皮袋终会裂开，酒自己就会流出来
proposed.ja: 古い革袋が破れてワインが自ら流れ出す

terms.gloss: old wineskins: worn institutions/containers that cannot hold the new
terms.why_hard: мехи is wineskins, not 'bellows' or 'fur coats', a common dictionary trap

terms.gloss: politics no longer manufactures compelling leaders
terms.why_hard: производит is industrial 'produce', not 'elect'; keep the factory metaphor

proposed.en: Politics does not produce interesting leaders
proposed.zh: 政治生产不出有意思的领袖
proposed.ja: 政治は面白い指導者を生み出さない

terms.gloss: Durov's label for founders who build mass civic products and thereby enter politics
terms.why_hard: Keep the English coinage or it becomes generic CSR/'stakeholder capitalism'

proposed.ja: アクティビスト・キャピタリズム

terms.gloss: shift in the information paradigm (how news/social data flow)
terms.why_hard: парадигма is Kuhn-lite tech talk, not 'information model' or 'media format'

terms.term: со всей возможной в четыре утра ясностью
terms.gloss: with all the clarity possible at four in the morning (exhausted-interview irony)
terms.why_hard: Keep the clock time; 'dawn' or 'late night' loses the 4 a.m. reportage beat

proposed.en: with all the clarity possible at four in the morning
proposed.zh: 在凌晨四点所能有的全部清醒里
proposed.ja: 午前四時に可能な限りの明晰さで

terms.gloss: The streams of people dried up — the crowds thinned as if a river ran dry, but only for two hours.
terms.why_hard: A literal rendering ('human flows dried') is incomprehensible; the river-drying image must be kept while making clear it means the crowd dispersed.

proposed.en: the streams of people ran dry

terms.gloss: Ironic epithet: Durov is likened to a seagull, a scruffy, opportunist St Petersburg bird; also echoes Chekhov's 'Seagull' emblem of the tortured creator.
terms.why_hard: Missing the seagull simile turns a sharp comic image into a plain description; it may also be a recurring epithet for Durov across the book.

proposed.en: a seagull by the name of Pavel Durov
proposed.zh: 一只名叫帕维尔·杜罗夫的海鸥
proposed.ja: パベル・ドゥーロフという名のカモメ

terms.gloss: Lurching along with one shoulder higher — a lopsided, self-important strut.
terms.why_hard: Flat 'walking crookedly' loses the mocking caricature of the entrepreneur's pose; this matches the 'seagull' satire and must stay comic.

terms.gloss: A French-style jacket with foam-padded shoulders — the uniform of 1990s Russian 'new Russians'/biznesmeny, deliberately oversized and comical.
terms.why_hard: Rendering as 'a coat with padded shoulders' loses the instantly recognisable 90s-gangster connotation for a Russian reader; needs an analogue, not a description.

proposed.en: a trench coat with foam-padded shoulders
proposed.zh: 垫着海绵厚肩的九十年代老板式大衣
proposed.ja: スポンジの肩パッドの入った90年代風ビジネスジャケット

terms.gloss: 'The new vine-growers' — the incoming generation of tech entrepreneurs who tend and reshape society; biblical/parable overtones of being given a new vineyard.
terms.why_hard: A literal 'new winemakers' reads as a non sequitur; the parable-like register (stewards of a new crop) must survive, and the phrase may recur as a book-level motif.

proposed.ja: 新しい葡萄園の耕し手

terms.gloss: Entrepreneurs now rival politicians, the state, and academia as producers of intellectual capacity — 'академия' means the academic world, not a specific school.
terms.why_hard: 'The academy' could be misread as a particular institution (e.g. an academy of sciences); it is the generic scholarly estate.

proposed.en: compete with politicians, the state, and academia
proposed.zh: 与政客、国家和学术界竞争
proposed.ja: 政治家や国家、アカデミアと競合する

terms.gloss: The colonnade of a St Petersburg hotel (in context, a landmark entrance where fans gathered — likely the Astoria near St Isaac's Square).
terms.why_hard: An unidentified 'hotel colonnade' disorients readers; translators must fix which hotel and keep its name consistent if it appears later in the book.

terms.gloss: The worn-out idols the fans are waiting for — earlier internet-era heroes (likely the older generation of web celebrities); 'кумир' carries pop-worship weight.
terms.why_hard: 'Old idols' can read as antiques or age; it means has-been celebrities of a previous wave, with a note of pity.

proposed.en: the idols of an earlier age

terms.gloss: A cardboard fan sign used as an umbrella — the standard fan-held placard at Russian public appearances.
terms.why_hard: 'Cardboard poster' should convey the makeshift fan placard (with a slogan for the idol), not a printed advertisement.

proposed.ja: 段ボール製の応援ボード

terms.gloss: first-year student, main developer of VK's Android app
terms.why_hard: real person's name transliteration must stay consistent across mentions

proposed.zh: 格里高利·克留什尼科夫
proposed.ja: グリゴリー・クリュシニコフ

terms.gloss: VKontakte, Russian social network founded by Durov
terms.why_hard: must use official branding consistently, not translate literally

terms.gloss: reference to a developer contest for VK's Android app
terms.why_hard: need to render as recognizable tech/product context, not overly literal

terms.gloss: guys obsessed/into mobile apps, period tech slang
terms.why_hard: casual slang 'угорать по' (to be really into something) needs equivalent register without sounding archaic

proposed.ja: モバイルアプリに熱中している

terms.gloss: slicked-back, mafia-looking men (visual stereotype of 2000s Russian business/crime elite)
terms.why_hard: cultural stereotype of post-Soviet 'mafiosi' look must be conveyed without literal 'mafia man' sounding cartoonish

proposed.zh: 梳得油光水滑的黑帮分子
proposed.ja: 髪を撫でつけたマフィアのような男たち

terms.gloss: shadowy figures in tailcoats and low-cut dresses, evoking hotel lobby elite ambiance
terms.why_hard: poetic register describing anonymous elegant crowd, easy to flatten into plain description

proposed.zh: 燕尾服与低胸礼服的身影
proposed.ja: 燕尾服とイブニングドレスの人影

terms.gloss: dumping, selling below value/market price
terms.why_hard: economic term used metaphorically for selling out cheaply; must keep consistent economic connotation

terms.gloss: "slavery, fleeing the battlefield" — Durov's metaphor for selling his stake
terms.why_hard: must preserve the martial/moral metaphor tone Durov is known for, not soften it

proposed.ja: 奴隷であり、戦場からの逃亡だ

terms.gloss: "not the Russian way" — appeal to national character/pride
terms.why_hard: carries implicit nationalist/cultural pride connotation that a flat translation loses

proposed.zh: 这不是俄罗斯人的做法

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte
terms.why_hard: surname alone must consistently refer to Pavel, not confused with brother Nikolai elsewhere in book

terms.gloss: first-year university student (implies youth, SPbU context)
terms.why_hard: conveys Russian university year system; should stay consistent with other academic-year references in book

terms.gloss: VKontakte's in-house coders/developers, salary benchmark
terms.why_hard: term 'кодеры' should be rendered consistently as 'coders/developers' throughout the book

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social network founded by Pavel Durov.
terms.why_hard: Book-wide decision: keep transliteration 'VKontakte' vs use 'VK', and quote-mark conventions differ by language.

terms.gloss: Mail.ru Group, the Russian internet holding company that owned Odnoklassniki and competed with VK.
terms.why_hard: Often conflated with the mail service; here it means the whole holding (холдинг), a distinction to keep consistent.

terms.gloss: Odnoklassniki ('Classmates'), the social network owned by Mail.ru, VK's main rival.

terms.gloss: Website or online platform, specifically VKontakte in this context
terms.why_hard: Literal 'resource' sounds like a natural resource in English; in Russian web slang of the 2000s it means a website or service

terms.gloss: Young working-class men associated with street culture, aggression, and tracksuits, viewed as uneducated and antisocial
terms.why_hard: Simply transliterating or translating as 'hooligans' misses the specific post-Soviet class and cultural connotations

terms.gloss: The state bureaucracy or government machinery responsible for public services and social policy
terms.why_hard: Careless translation might sound too neutral ('state apparatus') when the context implies Soviet-era bureaucratic inefficiency

terms.gloss: Capital of Russia, used here as a metonym for metropolitan Russia
terms.why_hard: Standard translation, but the contrast with provincial cities matters for the 'everywhere' argument

terms.gloss: Industrial city in Chelyabinsk Oblast, representing provincial Russia
terms.why_hard: English readers won't recognize it as a provincial Russian city; may need gloss or should be kept as-is to show the 'even in remote places' logic

terms.gloss: Major industrial city in the Urals where the speaker studied
terms.why_hard: Standard translation, but the speaker's personal connection ('where I studied') matters for ethos

terms.gloss: Redistribution of profits or resources, implying corruption and rent-seeking by officials
terms.why_hard: Could be translated too literally as economic policy when it really means officials lining their pockets

terms.gloss: Psychological manipulation of users, specifically for commercial or political ends
terms.why_hard: In internet context this specifically means dark patterns or deceptive UX design, not just general manipulation

terms.gloss: Society's progress toward modernity, civility, and better communication
terms.why_hard: Sounds like NGO jargon in English; here it means overcoming Soviet-era social backwardness

terms.gloss: Morally or ethically obsolete; backward in values and social norms
terms.why_hard: Could be read as 'old-fashioned morals' when it means the whole social system is obsolete

terms.gloss: Online reputation or social credit within the network
terms.why_hard: In Web 2.0 context this specifically means user ratings, reviews, and visible social standing

terms.gloss: Viral spread of information through social networks
terms.why_hard: Literal 'transmission speed' sounds like bandwidth; here it means how fast news/reputation damage spreads

terms.gloss: To socialize, communicate, or interact properly in civil society
terms.why_hard: Simple word, but the context implies 'communication skills' that gopniks allegedly lack

terms.gloss: University lecturers or school teachers, representing the educational establishment
terms.why_hard: Could be confused with 'professors' specifically, but Russian 'prepodavateli' includes secondary school teachers

terms.gloss: Places to hang out or spend leisure time, specifically youth recreational facilities
terms.why_hard: Formal Russian word for what English calls 'hangouts' or 'places to chill'; sounds bureaucratic if translated literally

terms.gloss: Overcoming physical distance through digital communication
terms.why_hard: Could sound like logistics; here it means connecting people across Russia's vast geography

terms.gloss: Users are sophisticated and cannot be easily fooled
terms.why_hard: Direct translation is fine, but the tone is defensive tech-idealism typical of early VK rhetoric

terms.gloss: Deceptive practices don't work well online due to transparency
terms.why_hard: Could be read as moral statement when it's actually a practical/business argument about viral backlash

terms.gloss: The entire social system is obsolete or broken
terms.why_hard: Russian 'morally obsolete' includes social norms, not just personal ethics

terms.gloss: Evolution or modernization of society through technology

terms.gloss: Those in power, the bureaucrats in government offices

terms.gloss: The point is; the real issue is

terms.gloss: A need or demand, specifically a social imperative for progress
terms.why_hard: Economic term used here for social evolution; don't translate as 'requirement' in the engineering sense

terms.gloss: Reasons or motivations for user behavior on the platform

terms.gloss: To meet someone halfway, to make a concession
terms.why_hard: A common Russian idiom meaning to accommodate or compromise; literal translation would be nonsensical

terms.gloss: Publishers/distributors in the media industry, here referring to film and music publishers

terms.gloss: Western (primarily Hollywood) film studios and distributors operating in Russia

terms.gloss: Record-breaking box office revenues in Russian cinemas
terms.why_hard: Refers specifically to theatrical box office, not general profits; a careless translation might miss the cinema-specific context

terms.gloss: Russian movie theaters/cinema chains
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered consistently with how Russian cinema infrastructure is described elsewhere in the book

terms.gloss: User-generated content platforms/websites

terms.gloss: American major film studios (the Big Six Hollywood studios)

proposed.ja: アメリカのメジャースタジオ

terms.gloss: Torrent files/sites (BitTorrent piracy networks)

terms.gloss: The film industry as a whole
terms.why_hard: Must be consistent with how the Russian film industry is referred to in other segments

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social network founded by Pavel Durov
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered consistently throughout the book; the choice between 'VKontakte', 'VK', or 'VK' affects tone

terms.gloss: A considerable amount of money; not a small sum
terms.why_hard: Understated Russian expression meaning 'a lot of money'; literal translation would sound awkward

terms.gloss: Living in the past century; hopelessly outdated

terms.gloss: The domain name of VKontakte as users would have typed it in the mid-2000s

terms.gloss: ICQ instant messenger, dominant in Russian internet culture in the mid-2000s

terms.gloss: Slang verb from 'ignore', meaning he'll ignore the message

terms.gloss: Informal collective noun for technical support staff

terms.gloss: Slang for administrators (of the site/community)

terms.gloss: Desktop computers, borrowed from English

terms.gloss: Short for ноутбуки (laptops), casual tech slang

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, the book's subject

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social network founded by Pavel Durov

notes: Невского: Standardized to 'Nevsky Prospekt' in English and '涅瓦大街' in Chinese as standard geographical designations.
Николай: Given name alone preserved as 'Nikolai' without interpolating the surname when absent from source.
Нёрды: Rendered as 'ギークたち' in Japanese and '极客们' in Chinese to capture tech subculture rather than mere bookishness.
Обломов: Stripped glosses/editorial adjectives across all languages to keep tone clean and uniform.
Одноклассники: Maintained brand transliteration across languages, adding parenthetical Chinese analogue once for audience clarity.
Петербург: Standardized to formal 'St. Petersburg' / 'サンクトペテルブルク' / '圣彼得堡' for consistency across chapters.
